title: Power loss for the local Mizohata--Takeuchi estimate on smooth hypersurfaces
authors: Hannah Cairo, Inbo Gottlieb Fenves, Vjekoslav Kovač, Itamar Oliveira, Dmitrii Zakharov, Ruixiang Zhang
abstract: We prove power-type lower bounds for the local Mizohata--Takeuchi constants for $C^{2,β}$ hypersurfaces with $0<β\leq1$ whose second fundamental form is nonzero at some point. This result, in particular, disproves the so-called local Mizohata--Takeuchi conjectures for the paraboloid and the sphere and, in turn, presents an obstruction to a general weighted approach to the theory of Fourier restriction of those classical surfaces.

title: Orbital differentiation in a rare earth ion near half filling
authors: D. W. Tam, Ø. S. Fjellvåg, B. Gonano, E. X. M. Trewick, M. Månsson
abstract: In the electronic structure of rare earth ions, details can be crucial for understanding the origin of correlated states. Currently, state-of-the-art wavefunction-based methods (e.g. CASSCF) can capture single-ion properties of molecular magnets and some band insulating systems, but are expensive to perform, and cannot be applied to metallic systems. Here, we carry out full multiplet calculations for SmN with the cubic rock-salt structure using the crystal field software Quanty. The calculated experimental observables from our model agree precisely with magnetic susceptibility and inelastic neutron scattering experiments, and the spatially resolved spin density also agrees with DFT predictions. By tuning the crystal field parameters, our full multiplet-derived wavefunctions reveal the presence of orbital differentiation of the ground $J=\frac{5}{2}$ manifold into two groups, which are distinct subspaces with different orbital stiffness. This violation of Hund's rule, observed with a fast and inexpensive calculation tool, represents a step forward for microscopic models of rare earth materials, and may provide support for the claim of unconventional triplet superconductivity in SmN.

title: Unveiling the mutual inclination distribution in astrometric surveys
authors: Jean-Baptiste Delisle
abstract: Mutual inclination in three (or more) body systems (triple stars, circumbinary planets, multi-planetary systems, etc.) is a tracer of their formation and evolution. Gaia Data Release 4 will provide for the first time a catalog of orbital solutions for three-body systems. Because astrometry is only sensitive to the motion in the plane of the sky, there is a degeneracy in the orbital solutions leading to two possible solutions for the mutual inclination in three-body systems. We propose a hierarchical Bayesian framework to circumvent this degeneracy and unveil the mutual inclination distribution in the population. We tested our methods on simulated datasets, and showed that it reliably recovered the injected mutual inclination distributions in various cases. The method is thus promising for the statistical analysis of Gaia DR4 three-body systems.

title: VoxelSBFL: Voxel-Level Spectrum-Based Failure Prediction for Vision-Language-Action Models
authors: Arusa Kanwal, Pablo Valle, Paola Roggero, Miren Illarramendi, Shaukat Ali, Aitor Arrieta
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models integrate visual perception, language understanding, and action generation to control robots. Testing these systems produces trajectories and task outcomes, but existing approaches provide limited guidance on using these recorded trajectories to assess subsequent executions or inform policy repair. We conjecture that, for a given policy and task, traversing certain workspace regions is associated with a higher likelihood of failure. To investigate this conjecture, we propose VoxelSBFL, a black-box adaptation of Spectrum-Based Fault Localization (SBFL) in which workspace voxels replace program elements as units of analysis. Recorded tool-center-point (TCP) trajectories provide binary voxel coverage, which is combined with execution outcomes to construct suspiciousness maps using established SBFL formulas. These maps identify failure-associated regions and score unseen trajectories without requiring internal model access. We evaluate 34 spectrum-based techniques across four VLA models using 96,000 Pick-Up trajectories in simulation and compare the leading techniques against eight action- and trajectory-based metrics. VoxelSBFL obtains an overall macro ROC-AUC of 0.704, significantly outperforming state-of-the art baselines. Sensitivity analyses show that performance varies with spatial granularity and training-set size. These findings support spatial spectra for VLA execution assessment and motivate future research on runtime monitoring, self-healing and targeted policy improvement.

title: Anti-aging Squeezed Quantum Battery
authors: Jing-Ci Yue, Jing-Tao Tang, Jun-Hong An
abstract: Exhibiting the superiority of energy storage and conversion over its classical counterpart, quantum battery (QB) emerges as a promising platform to revolutionize traditional energy technologies. However, their practical performance is severely constrained by the ubiquitous decoherence in microscopic world, which causes rapid aging and reduced ergotropy. Here, we propose a decoherence-tolerant QB consisting of a continuous-variable bosonic mode. Acting as the quantum resource, the utilized squeezing endows the QB with unprecedented energy capacity and ergotropy. Through investigating the non-Markovian decoherence effect on the QB, we find that such squeezing enhanced performance can be persistently preserved under the influence of decoherence as long as a bound state is present in the energy spectrum of the total system formed by the QB and the environment. This decoherence-tolerance feature is even maintained under moderate finite-temperature condition. Providing a useful energy storage paradigm for designing long-lived QBs, our result sheds light on the realization of anti-aging QBs.

title: Autonomous Track Racing with a Commercially Available Humanoid: System Design and Real-World Deployment
authors: Koki Inami, Takashi Sato, Hiroyuki Oka, Shota Takizawa, Yuya Takahashi, Amon Suzuki, Hayato Ono, Kohtaro Ihara, Yuki Noka, Shohei Matsugu
abstract: Learning-based methods now let humanoids run robustly, and they have begun to compete in athletic events. Yet few reports describe a complete autonomous humanoid running system in an actual race, where the robot must follow a lane at a new venue, pace itself within hardware limits, and finish without intervention. We report such a system deployed on the Unitree G1, a commercially available general-purpose humanoid, in the 100 m, 400 m, and 1500 m events of the World Humanoid Robot Games 2026. The system integrates vision-based lane perception, path tracking, and a running policy trained by reinforcement learning with a human motion prior. To address the challenges of humanoid running, we stabilize head-camera images against body motion and use IMU-assisted leg odometry to bridge flight phases. To manage motor heating, we penalize hip-pitch torque during training, add heat-dissipation plates, and apply temperature-based speed limiting with event-specific pacing. The robot placed 13th of 74 in the 100 m, 10th of 44 in the 400 m first round before falling in the semifinal, and seventh of 35 in the 1500 m. In this deployment, thermal margin set the pace in every event, and the semifinal fall followed a lane-detection error.

title: Multilevel Filtering on Manifolds with Light Schrödinger Bridges
authors: Jason Beh, Pierre Del Moral, Ajay Jasra
abstract: In this article we consider the filtering of partially observed diffusions when the observations, made at discrete times, are noiseless. Each observation then confines the hidden state to a manifold defined by the data, whose type, for instance a sphere or an affine subspace, may change from one observation time to the next. In practice, the filter is approximated by particle filters, which require the diffusion to be discretized in time. Multilevel Monte Carlo reduces the cost of this discretization only if the particle approximations at consecutive discretization levels stay close, which standard particle filters do not ensure. We develop a new particle filter based on light Schrödinger bridges, which works between changing manifolds and can be coupled across discretization levels. A key insight is that the previous state enters the light Schrödinger bridge only through a few features, so that the bridge only has to be fitted on the new manifold, regardless of the type of the previous one. We bound the bias of this particle filter and the gap between its approximations at consecutive levels, and show numerically, on spheres and on manifolds that change type, that this gap is much smaller than with standard multilevel particle filters, and that, with the cost of the fits included, a hybrid estimator that uses it at the fine levels reduces the cost at small tolerances.

title: Magnetic History and Field Sweep Rate Effects on Transformation Hysteresis in $\mathrm{Ni}_{41}\mathrm{Co}_{9}\mathrm{Mn}_{31.5}\mathrm{Ga}_{18.5}$
authors: T. Kihara, T. Miyakawa, D. Imatomi, X. Xu, Y. Ishii, H. Hayashi, Y. H. Matsuda, Y. Adachi, T. Kanomata
abstract: Hysteresis in magnetic-field-induced structural phase transformations is a major obstacle to the application of metamagnetic shape memory alloys. One promising approach to reduce hysteresis is to utilize a metastable martensitic state generated by magnetic-field cycling. However, the mechanism by which the metastable state reduces hysteresis remains unclear. Here, microsecond pulsed-field magnetization measurements are used to investigate the transformation kinetics of $\mathrm{Ni}_{41}\mathrm{Co}_{9}\mathrm{Mn}_{31.5}\mathrm{Ga}_{18.5}$. Magnetic-field cycling reduces the hysteresis width by approximately 50-60%, demonstrating that substantial suppression persists on a microsecond timescale. Comparison with millisecond pulsed-field measurements suggests that the reverse martensitic transformation field is more sensitive to the field sweep rate for the metastable martensite than for the initial martensite. Possible explanations include enhanced thermal activation associated with a lower effective activation barrier and differences in the athermal contribution arising from different metastable martensitic microstructures.

title: On the Kissing Number of Craig's Lattice and Spherical List Decoding
authors: Léo Ducas, Julian Nowakowski, Ailsa Robertson
abstract: Craig's lattices $A_{p-1}^k$ are a family of lattices with large kissing numbers, i.e., relative to their dimension $n = p-1$, they contain a large number of shortest nonzero vectors. Specifically, for small $k = o(\log p / \log \log p)$, a lower bound of Bacher (2015) shows that $A_{p-1}^k$ has a super-polynomial kissing number of $ω(n^k)$. Craig's lattices are therefore attractive candidates for the construction of spherical codes. In this work, we introduce a polynomial-time list decoder for spherical codes obtained from Craig's lattices for angular distance below $45^\circ$. Our second main result shows that Bacher's lower bound is asymptotically tight for $k = o(\log p / \log \log p)$. Finally, we introduce an efficient algorithm for computing the kissing number of $A_{p-1}^k$. Using this algorithm, we compute their kissing number in dimensions up to 521. Based on this data, we pose the open question whether the kissing number of $A_{p-1}^k$ with $k \approx \sqrt{p}$ grows like $e^{Θ(\sqrt{n})}$ in dimension $n=p-1$. Concurrent work by Laarhoven and Kominers as well as Bennett, Hhan, Li and Stephens-Davidowitz proves such a bound for very closely related lattices.

title: Normalized solutions for logarithmic $p$-Laplacian equations on graphs
authors: Wenyuan Ma, Anfeng Yuan
abstract: We study a logarithmic $p$-Laplacian equation with prescribed $L^2$ mass on connected locally finite weighted graphs, with $p > 2$. By minimizing the energy, we obtain a positive solution for every prescribed mass $m > 0$ on finite graphs and, under additional assumptions on the vertex measure and the potential, on infinite graphs. We describe the behavior of positive solutions and their Lagrange multipliers as $m \to 0^+$ or $m \to +\infty$. In particular, as $m \to 0^+$, the minimizers rescaled to unit mass converge along subsequences to functions supported at a single vertex.

title: Confinement Alters Energy Relaxation in Subrecoil Laser Cooling
authors: Daiki Kanbe, Eli Barkai, Takuma Akimoto
abstract: Controlling atomic motion through laser cooling requires both reducing kinetic energy and confining atoms to a finite spatial region. Here, we investigate how harmonic confinement modifies the long-time energy relaxation in subrecoil laser cooling. Using a stochastic scattering-rate model, numerical simulations, and an analytically tractable renewal approximation, we show that confinement qualitatively changes the asymptotic relaxation law. For a scattering rate that vanishes at low momentum as $R(p)\propto |p|^α$, the change arises because confinement reshapes the phase-space geometry of rare, long trapping events. In free space, such events require only small momentum. Under harmonic confinement, however, position and momentum are coupled along phase-space orbits, restricting long-lived low-scattering trajectories to the vicinity of the phase-space origin. This geometric constraint modifies the trapping-time statistics, produces two dynamical crossovers, and leads to an optimal scattering-rate exponent of $α=4$ for the fastest asymptotic decay of the mean energy. Our results demonstrate that confinement changes the asymptotic energy-relaxation dynamics even when the local scattering law remains unchanged.

title: Generating Massive Mechanical Superpositions through Qubit-Mediated Interference
authors: José P. Dupont, Loek van Everdingen, Tjerk H. Oosterkamp, Louk Rademaker
abstract: We propose a method towards demonstrating a quantum superposition of a massive mechanical resonator without the need for exact ground-state cooling, a requirement that becomes increasingly difficult to satisfy for low-frequency resonators. Our scheme relies on coupling the resonator to a spin-qubit. Using magnetic force coupling between the motion of the mechanical resonator and the spin-qubit, the resonator is forced into attracted and repelled states as the spin-qubit is coherently controlled. Interference between the resonator states can be observed when a series of $\tfracπ{2}$-pulses is applied to the spin-qubit within the coherence time of the resonator. The protocol describes a true which-path interference experiment suitable for use at ultra-low temperatures, since it requires only three $\tfracπ{2}$-pulses, separated in time by half a mechanical period, thus minimizing the heat-load and duration of the experiment. By analysing the experimental requirements necessary to successfully execute the protocol, we show that the protocol is suitable for resonators in a broad regime of resonance frequencies, ranging from 1kHz resonators, which have the advantage of a relatively high spin-coupling, to resonators of more than 100kHz, whose mechanical mode is easier to cool. We show that interference remains visible for resonator mode occupations exceeding 10 phonons. Lastly, we observe that an implementation of the protocol with low-frequency mechanical resonators provides a promising approach towards testing objective collapse models.

title: Symbolic Abstraction Refinement
authors: Daniel Bryce, Robert P. Goldman, David J. Musliner, Jeremy Gottlieb, John Skovbekk
abstract: Autonomous systems choose actions whose outcomes are uncertain and are subject to time constraints. Probabilistic timed automata (PTAs) model exactly this, and verifying one answers a question about the system's decision-making: the maximum probability of reaching a goal, or the minimum probability of reaching a hazard, that a controller can guarantee. Verification normally works over symbolic states, each pairing a discrete location with a region of clock values, and its difficulty is that the best behavior generally varies within such a region. The PRISM verifier's most capable PTA method responds by splitting regions until each is uniform, rebuilding the transitions that reach them and propagating the split backward through the state graph of a stochastic game, a cascade of graph reconstruction that partitions regions the property never depends on. We present SYMAR, which instead makes the value function symbolic: each symbolic state carries a function from sub-regions of its clock region to probability bounds, so refinement is the appearance of new sub-regions in that function, and previously generated states are never split nor their incoming transitions reconstructed. Both sources of PTA nondeterminism, the timing and the choice of actions, are captured implicitly by the preimage computation that produces those sub-regions. Heuristic forward search then bounds how much refinement is done at all, expanding an And-Or graph from the initial state along the most promising behaviors so that effort is confined to the property-relevant fragment, guided by bounds and preferred actions from a single unrefined run of the existing method; a partial-refinement backup keeps the otherwise combinatorial sub-region count lean, and every stored interval provably contains the true probability. On the PRISM PTA benchmarks, whose subproblems recur in autonomous systems (distributed agreement under contention, leader election, and self-configuration without central coordination), SYMAR is up to 108x faster, solves an instance on which the existing method exhausts the time limit, and is markedly less sensitive to the deadline constant, resolving one instance in a 37-node search graph, unchanged as the deadline triples, where the existing method needs 86,380 abstract states and 73 refinement rounds.

title: RyBench: Runtime Verification Benchmarking Framework over Publish/Subscribe Networks
authors: Mehmet Hilmi Dündar, Doğan Ulus
abstract: Autonomous systems built as distributed, node-based systems communicate via publish/subscribe middleware. Runtime Verification (RV) tools are used to monitor those systems against formal specifications, receiving monitored events through the pub/sub channel. An RV tool's practical value depends on its monitoring throughput capacity and verdict latency, besides its correctness, so a systematic benchmarking setup is needed to evaluate how efficiently these tools run. This paper presents RyBench, a pub/sub-based benchmarking framework that acts as a synthetic event publisher in place of a monitored system, providing a common benchmarking setup. RyBench separates benchmark generation, serialization, and transport into distinct components, enabling the combination of different event-generation strategies, data formats, and transport layers. We also evaluate the framework's throughput capacity across these configurations using Open Simulation Interface (OSI) schemas and Timescales properties, and illustrate the end-to-end benchmarking flow through an application to Reelay and an integration with MonPoly.

title: From Constraints to Causality: Petri net Encodings for Explaining Binary Neural Network Inference
authors: Alex Chan, Mohamed Tarraf, Alex Yakovlev, Rishad Shafik
abstract: Binary Neural Networks (BNNs) are attractive for resource-constrained hardware and on-device components in autonomous systems. However, their discrete, non-linear behaviour makes them difficult to analyse and trust in safety-relevant settings. Existing approaches based on SAT and Satisfiability Modulo Theories can verify a BNN's input-output properties, but treat it as a monolithic constraint system, which reveal only whether a property holds and not how the computation reaches its result. In this paper, we present an early work that provides a complementary, discrete-event view. We give a compositional translation from the inference semantics of a fixed, trained BNN to a 1-safe Petri net (PN), where each computation step is an explicit transition, so that a firing sequence is a causal trace of the BNN's decision. On a worked example, we establish faithfulness via exhaustive input-output equivalence against a reference implementation, and show how contrasting firing sequences localises where a single-feature change alters the prediction. Finally, we outline two directions this opens: a correctness-of-translation theorem, and a causal-trace analysis of where two trained BNNs diverge in their decisions, a structural question that constraint-based verifiers cannot express.

title: Formal Analysis of a Fault-Tolerant Extension of the ROSACE Flight Controller
authors: Marco Bozzano, Alessandro Cimatti, Moussa Fall, Stefano Tonetta
abstract: Autonomous avionics controllers must satisfy stringent real-time functional and performance require- ments even in the presence of run-time faults. In this paper, we analyze ROSACE, an open-source control engineering benchmark for flight control systems, focusing on its run-time resilience against faults such as sensor noise and sensor failures. We extend the benchmark with an FDIR (Fault Detection, Identification and Recovery) component based on Triple Modular Redundancy. Our approach builds upon COMPASTA, a tool for Model-Based Design developed on top of the TASTE tool by ESA. COMPASTA enables the modeling and injection of faults into a system's design. Moreover, it implements a simulation-based verification and validation workflow, automating the generation and execution of a set of test cases, based on a user-defined notion of coverage. Using COMPASTA, we construct a set of formal models, with faults and with FDIR, and we formally analyze their impact on the system properties. The analysis is based on the coupling of the formal models with the Simulink models used for the simulations.

title: Development and Validation of a preCICE Based OpenMOC OpenFOAM Coupling Framework for Nuclear Reactor Analysis
authors: Seth S. W. Choo, L. K. Ang, Zhe Chuan Tan
abstract: To address the long computation time required by stochastic solvers, which are applied in the coupled neutronics-thermal hydraulics (N-TH) calculations, a faster N-TH coupling framework is developed based on the multiphysics coupling library preCICE, which enables data exchange between OpenMOC and OpenFOAM. As an alternative to commonly used stochastic solvers, like OpenMC, OpenMOC is used as a neutronics solver providing much faster steady-state solution in a Picard iteration. To realize this coupling strategy, OpenMC is used for an initial one-time computation cost for multi-group cross sections data generation that is used throughout OpenMOC calculations. A preCICE library adapter for OpenMOC is also developed, allowing data exchange between neutronic power distributions and thermal hydraulic temperature fields. Our proposed coupling framework is validated through simulations of a simplified 2 times 2 fuel assembly, and a quartered geometry of 17 times 17 fuel assembly. The comparison shows good agreement with established referenced solutions, highlighting our proposed coupling framework for the steady-state N-TH coupling at a fraction of the time required by stochastic solver codes. This advantages could be extended for future applications where fast approximated solutions are required to address the change of N-TH coupling due to small parametric changes like in digital twin of nuclear reactor.

title: Bent-tailed radio galaxies as tracers of the intrafilament medium
authors: Katlego Morakile, Kshitij Thorat, Etienne Bonnassieux, Tiziana Venturi, Konstantinos Kolokythas
abstract: Bent-tailed radio galaxies have traditionally been associated with, and used as tracers of, the dense intracluster medium. In recent years, however, such sources have also been identified outside of clusters, with only a few discovered in low-density environments of cosmic filaments. Their occurrence in low-density environments remains rare and is still poorly understood. We announce the discovery of bent-tailed radio galaxies in galaxy cluster filaments. We have identified two bent-tailed radio galaxies, J0020-25 and J0019-26, within a filament at the redshift of $z \sim 0.1273$, and another bent-tailed radio galaxy, J0019-25, in a separate filament at $z \sim 0.1126$. We used MeerKAT observations of these bent-tailed radio galaxies to place constraints on their intrafilament medium (IFM). The effects of the filaments could be seen in the radio morphologies of these galaxies. Using faint regions in each galaxy, we estimate the intrafilament pressure, density, magnetic field strength, and total energy density. We found an IFM density of $ρ_\text{IFM} \approx 3.8\times 10^{-29}$ g cm$^{-3}$ for the surrounding medium of J0020-25 and J0019-26, and $ρ_\text{IFM} \approx (0.2 - 1.1) \times 10^{-26}$ g cm$^{-3}$ around J0019-25. We found that our estimates for the intrafilament environment around J0020-25 and J0019-26 lie within the $ρ_\text{IFM}$ literature estimates, while the density estimate found using J0019-25 is higher than the literature density estimates for the IFM and in agreement with the density of group environments. J0019-25 likely resides in a galaxy group embedded within a filament. These discoveries show the capabilities of using bent-tailed radio galaxies as probes to locate the otherwise invisible large-scale filaments.

title: AutoE2E: Don't speak - Language free end-to-end autonomy A Real-Time Driving Model for L2++ ADAS and L4 Robotaxis
authors: Muhammad Zain Khawaja, Zaynab El Mawas, Ryota Yamada, Gabriela Cordova, Arseni Lysak, Intisar Chowdhury, Bharat Jayaprakash, Apostolos Georgiadis, Shri Harsha Adapala, Jatin Gautam, Christoph Bank, Alejandra Solarte Uscategui, Atanasko Boris Mitrev, Hassan Ali Ansari, Nishad Sahu
abstract: AutoE2E is an open-source end-to-end driving model developed by the Autoware Foundation Robotaxi Working Group. It introduces a temporal bird's-eye-view (BEV) architecture that combines multi-camera perception, HD-map information and route conditioning to predict future vehicle motion. The evaluated model uses a pretrained camera-BEV backbone, temporal feature fusion and a lightweight recurrent trajectory planner. It contains approximately 79.9 million parameters, of which approximately 1.45 million are trainable in the evaluated configuration. The v1.0 release provides model checkpoints, training and evaluation code, and DataModelConsole, a dashboard for visualizing and inspecting model experiments. On the KITScenes validation benchmark, the fine-tuned checkpoint achieves an average displacement error (ADE) of 0.745 m and a final displacement error (FDE) of 2.020 m at a three-second prediction horizon. The paper also reports preliminary real-vehicle research conducted with the Technical University of Munich's EDGAR platform, alongside ongoing collaboration with the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology. AutoE2E v1.0 is an early open research release. Its quantitative evaluation is open-loop, and the model has not yet demonstrated validated closed-loop autonomous driving. The release is intended to provide the autonomous-driving community with an inspectable baseline for further research, experimentation and collaborative development.

title: HiGAI-Net: Hierarchical Encrypted Traffic Classification for Generative AI Services
authors: Madhan Raj Kanagarathinam, Jaheon Gu, Krishna M. Sivalingam, Kapal Dev
abstract: The Radio Access Network (RAN) today does not have a reliable way to identify GenAI traffic (ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot, or Google Gemini traffic) at the bearer level. TLS~1.3 moves SNI into the encrypted handshake record, and Encrypted ClientHello (ECH) removes it entirely from passive inspection; Gemini has partly shifted to QUIC where SNI visibility also depends on whether ECH is deployed. Without per-flow application identity, differentiated QoS for GenAI services is not possible. HiGAI-Net tackles this using only packet-header metadata, stacking three independently trained classifiers: a binary AI/Non-AI gate (98.5 % weighted F1), a per-service resolver across ChatGPT, Copilot, and Gemini (86.4 %), and a text-vs-voice/video mode classifier (61.0 %). The core innovation is a suite of sliding-window temporal features that track how DL/UL byte-ratios evolve within a session -- the per-quarter and per-half ratio trends, a trend differential $ΔR$, and a streaming regularity index. Tested on 44,492 labeled flows, gradient-boosted tree models consistently outperformed all deep-learning variants; a per-flow label cache brings amortised inference below 1~$μ$s per packet.

title: What makes the gravito-thermodynamic arrow of time coincide with that of proper time?
authors: Samarjit Chakraborty, Rituparno Goswami
abstract: In the pursuit of a geometrical resolution to this important question for the evolution of spherically symmetric perfect fluids in general relativity, we excavated a novel result: the presence of volume distortions and inhomogeneities are, though necessary, but not sufficient for the total gravitational entropy to monotonically increase with proper time. We need a further refinement of the space of distortions and only those that favour shell crossing caustics, causing local flocculations and structure formations, can ensure the alignment. This result will have far reaching consequences for the study of thermodynamical viability of various gravitational collapse and cosmological solutions of Einstein field equations.

title: Explicit Dual Model Predictive Path Integral Control
authors: Christopher Narr, Martin Buss
abstract: In this work, we present a fully sampling-based explicit dual control algorithm that combines a particle filter and model predictive path integral control for partially observed nonlinear systems. The key idea is to roll out multiple sampled input sequences from all particles of the particle filter to obtain a belief-averaged control cost that induces caution. The same rollouts are used to sample imagined future measurements, which are drawn from the predictive distribution of the particle belief. This results in a Monte Carlo information term that gives a sample estimate of the expected information gain of each sampled input sequence and thereby induces probing. In contrast to existing explicit dual control schemes, the proposed scheme neither relies on gradients of the dynamics or measurement models nor requires a Gaussian belief. Furthermore, all computations can be parallelized across input sequences, particles, and imagined measurements, which makes the scheme amenable to real-time implementation on suitable hardware. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in a simulation example of a planar terrain-aided navigation task.

title: Seeing What Still Holds: How Waiting Control Changes Cooperative Recovery
authors: Kangjie Huang, Yucheng Xin, Xinchun Wang, Dong Liu, Yan Fan, Shuming Liu
abstract: Changing the holding reference during a fixed-duration wait can reverse the ranking of visual recovery methods. We introduce AuditEmbodied, a paired execution and trajectory evaluation framework that independently varies holding references and waiting duration while keeping recovery executors frozen. A 960-execution factorial on 20 initialization seeds compares CAD-feedback and landmark-based recovery from identical post-wait physical states within each holding and waiting condition. Protected completion requires successful recovery under the declared execution constraints. At a 1 s wait with registered wrist references, their protected completion counts change from 6/40 versus 19/40 under registered holding to 34/40 versus 22/40 under position-only holding. Trajectory analysis localizes the main separation to grasp formation: small observation-time target residuals precede large tracking errors. Joint diagnostics and controlled interventions characterize persistent tracking constraints. On fresh seeds, gradual position reanchoring improves CAD recovery's long-wait completion by 42.5 percentage points and reduces mean complete recovery time by 6.06 s relative to registered holding. Additional evaluations with pretrained policies, handover, and a mass-matched geometry characterize holding-reference sensitivity across executors and physical regimes. These findings establish holding reference as an explicit evaluation condition for comparing visual recovery performance.

title: Topological Timing of Bound States by Spacetime Mass Windings
authors: Hamdi Barkaoui
abstract: Topology usually determines where a wave is trapped. Here we show that it can also determine when a trapped state brightens or dims. We consider a dimerized photonic lattice in which a real Dirac mass, varying in space, binds a Jackiw-Rebbi state, while staggered gain and loss, switched in time, act as an imaginary Dirac mass on that same state. Together, the two masses form a mass field in space and time whose isolated zeros carry an integer winding. Combining a continuum Dirac description with finite-lattice simulations, we show that the sign of this winding fixes whether the bound state reaches a maximum or a minimum at the switch, while the gain and loss remain below the bulk gap. The windings obey a conservation law: they are created and annihilated in pairs, and their sum along a boundary determines which extrema are protected. Full-wave simulations of a passive waveguide array, in which the propagation distance plays the role of time, reproduce these predictions with loss alone. These results provide a topological handle on the timing of localized optical responses, relevant to switching, gating, and pulse shaping of confined modes in integrated photonic circuits and topological lasers.

title: Data-driven model reduction: An identification perspective using Generalized Bases of Orthonormal Functions
authors: Bernard Vau, Henri Bourlès
abstract: This paper proposes a data-driven model order reduction approach based on system identification concepts. A revised equation error formulation is introduced, in which the model is parameterized using Generalized Bases of Orthonormal Transfer Functions (GBOFs). The generalized reduction problem is formulated in the Hambo frequency domain associated with the GBOF transform. The frequency-domain fit of the reduced-order model is adjusted through the selection of the basis poles. A fit indicator depending on these poles is introduced, providing valuable heuristic guidance for their selection.

title: NONSENSE: Non-Semantic Strings Expose Semanticity Gaps in Dense Retrieval
authors: Ankit Gupta
abstract: Dense retrieval is central to modern search, question answering, and retrieval-augmented generation, where high similarity is often treated as evidence of semantic relevance. We examine how far this assumption can be stressed. NONSENSE is a black-box sparse-edit probe that constructs visibly non-semantic strings while forbidding query-term copying, optimizing only the dense similarity between a query and the string. Across five BEIR-style datasets and three popular single-vector retrievers, these strings frequently outscore the retriever's own best judged query-relevant passage (QRP), and often rank first in the full corpus. The result indicates a semanticity gap in the evaluated dense retrievers: nearest-neighbor status can be separated from passage-like meaning. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating dense retrievers not only by whether they retrieve relevant documents, but also by how reliably their similarity scores reflect semantic evidence.

title: Scaling Laws for Vision-Language Fusion
authors: Seng Pei Liew, Teppei Suzuki, Seiya Tokui
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have emerged as central foundation models combining multimodal perception with text comprehension. While VLMs are traditionally built via late fusion by continued pre-training an off-the-shelf language model on multimodal (image-text) data, mixing modalities from the start of pre-training (early fusion) has recently gained traction. However, the fundamental trade-offs between these paradigms remain poorly understood, resulting in expensive and heuristic-driven training recipes. In this paper, we systematically analyze the learning dynamics of these multimodal pre-training processes, showing that validation losses during vision-language fusion can be modeled by separating the base learning trajectory, where different data types contribute at distinct rates, from a distribution shift driven by the competition between modalities. We derive a scaling law that unifiedly describes these dynamics, enabling accurate loss predictions across mixture ratios, training steps, and model sizes. Crucially, our law characterizes the trade-off between early and late fusion: under a fixed data budget, early fusion preserves text performance while late fusion favors vision performance, yielding a trade-off that increasingly tilts toward early fusion as model size scales. Extensive experiments confirm that our scaling law reliably captures multimodal learning dynamics and governs fusion decisions.

title: Small Area Causal Inference
authors: Yilin Li, Jiangshan Zhang, Jiming Jiang
abstract: We develop a framework for small area causal inference (SACI). Unlike the traditional doubly robust (DR) estimation approach, the new framework is based on the empirical best prediction (EBP) method. EBP takes into consideration not only the bias but also the variance factor, which is often a more dominant component in the mean squared prediction error (MSPE). Under a linear mixed model for SACI, we establish consistency and asymptotic normality of the maximum likelihood estimator of the model parameters. More relevant to our main objective, we establish asymptotic optimality of the EBP in terms of minimizing the MSPE of the area-specific causal-effect (ASCE) predictor. Moreover, in view of the traditional interest in causal inference, we establish asymptotic normality of the EBP of the ASCE , which is used to construct prediction intervals for the ASCEs. We carry out extensive simulation studies to investigate finite-sample performance of the proposed EBP and its comparison with the traditional DR and other existing methods. Our simulation results show that the proposed EBP method has significant advantage over the comparing methods in terms of MSPE and coverage probability and length of the resulting prediction interval. A real-data example from agricultural-animal genetics is discussed.

title: Reliable Evaluation of AI Agents for Investment Research: A Framework for Performance and Validity Assessment
authors: Dongnuan Tian, Yan Yu, Yangfan Liu, Wenjun Tang, Junting Kan, Xiang Wang, Sicong Liu, Yangyang Zhang, Shuanghong Li
abstract: We consider the problem of evaluating AI agents undertaking investment-research tasks, where agents interact with external information sources and computational tools to produce financial analyses and research reports. An important challenge is that the quality of an agent's final output does not necessarily reflect the quality of its execution process, while the reliability of the resulting assessment also depends on the validity of the evaluation procedure. Furthermore, investment-research tasks differ considerably in their requirements for numerical accuracy, information retrieval, financial analysis and supporting evidence, making it difficult to assess agent performance using a uniform set of criteria. We propose a domain-oriented evaluation framework that distinguishes outcome quality from execution quality and accommodates these differences through task-specific criteria, deterministic validators and independent large language model judges. We also introduce an evaluation-validity mechanism that examines the integrity of evaluation inputs, reference information, supporting evidence and grading outputs, with expert review used to resolve identified deficiencies and significant grading disagreements. Numerical results show that the proposed framework can distinguish differences in agent performance across evaluation dimensions, while identifying potential reliability issues in the evaluation process. The associated implementation and evaluation materials will be made available on GitHub.

title: Complex mobility edges from competing localization channels in non-Hermitian quasicrystals
authors: Bing Shao, Weiwei Zhu, Longwen Zhou
abstract: Non-Hermitian localization transitions often accompany multiple mobility edges, but their physical origin can be ambiguous. To address the issue, we introduce an extension of the Ganeshan-Pixley-Das Sarma model with both asymmetric hopping and complex onsite potential, thereby incorporating a broad range of non-Hermitian quasiperiodic chains. Its solution reveals two energy-dependent localization contributions manifested as distinct Lyapunov growth scales, whose competition determines the structure of mobility edges. We derive exact Lyapunov exponents via Avila's global theory, obtain thresholds of the two channels on complex-energy plane, and formulate a selection rule that distinguishes physical mobility edges from suppressed analytical candidates. The channel that uniquely controls localization can switch with energy, producing complex mobility edges of non-Hermitian origins. Nonreciprocal hopping further shifts the thresholds and alters the bulk energy patterns. Numerical spectra and finite-size localization diagnostics confirm the theory. Our work thus provides a unified framework for characterizing phase transitions and mobility edges under competing localization mechanisms in non-Hermitian quasicrystals.

title: MoL-SQL: A Controlled Benchmark for Mixture-of-Language Text-to-SQL
authors: Tianqi Luo, Boyan Li, Yuyu Luo
abstract: Text-to-SQL systems are usually built and evaluated under a monolingual assumption, yet in international applications users often query databases stored in a different language. Existing multilingual benchmarks mostly translate only the question without aligning schema and value entities, so they can neither locate the source of an accuracy drop nor rule out translation errors. Hence, we introduce MoL-SQL, a benchmark for mixture-of-language Text-to-SQL that switches the languages of the question, schema, and stored values independently while keeping each task fixed, and grades every cross-lingual entity mapping into four difficulty levels. We migrate five Text-to-SQL benchmarks of different domains and source languages through a unified alignment pipeline that builds a shared cross-lingual entity map, migrates each database with its constraints, rewrites the gold SQL under execution-equivalence checks, and regenerates the question from the verified SQL, keeping all language versions of a task aligned in entities, intent, and execution result. MoL-SQL provides two splits: MoL-Full (16,892 samples) for overall evaluation and MoL-Cube (3,840 samples) covering every language combination to isolate question, schema, and value effects. Experiments with eight LLMs and four families of Text-to-SQL methods show that schema and value languages have distinct effects, with stored values costing up to 23 points, and that these effects mainly stem from cross-lingual entity mapping. Neither question translation nor additional reasoning narrows the value gap, whereas access to target-database values substantially reduces it, indicating that mixture-of-language Text-to-SQL benefits most from language-aware context grounding.

title: Mapping phase competition in GaAs under pressure and temperature
authors: Sakshi Patel, Paras Patel, Prafulla K. Jha
abstract: Pressure-induced transformations in GaAs offer a means to investigate the interplay between crystal structure, electronic behaviour, and phase stability in a technologically important III-V semiconductor. Here, we have used structure search algorithm combined with first-principles calculations and identified high-pressure competitive phases. The previously proposed $Imm2$ structure lies above the calculated minimum-enthalpy envelope. The static enthalpy calculations with the PBEsol functional predict the transition sequence $F\bar{4}3m \rightarrow Cmcm \rightarrow I\bar{4}m2 \rightarrow C2/m \rightarrow Amm2$, at approximately 12, 14, 34, and 69 GPa, respectively. The initial zinc blende to $Cmcm$ transition is accompanied by a volume reduction of approximately 17.5 % and metallization within the PBEsol description. Phonon calculations support the dynamical stability of all five phases at representative pressures, while elastic calculations characterize their mechanical response. Vibrational free energies are incorporated within the quasiharmonic approximation to examine phase competition over 0-80 GPa and 0-1000 K. These results identify competing high-pressure structures and connect their relative energetics with the electronic, vibrational, and elastic responses of compressed GaAs.

title: DAP-MR: Degradation-Aware Prompt-Magnitude Routing for Real-World Ultrasound Super-Resolution
authors: Ngoc-Hoang-Lam Le, Thi-An Le, Dinh-Hung Le, Manh-Hung Nguyen, Kai-Lung Hua, Ching-Chun Huang
abstract: When super-resolution models designed for natural images are used on ultrasound scans, relying on semantic text prompts can lead to unreliable results. The tags these models generate often do not match the actual restoration needs, and specialized medical terms may be misunderstood by general-purpose text encoders. Instead, prompts focused on common image degradations are more directly useful for guiding restoration. However, using a single prompt to describe both the type and severity of image degradation can entangle these factors, making it hard for the model to know how strong the degradation is. To address this limitation, we introduce Degradation-Aware Prompt--Magnitude Routing (DAP-MR). Each degradation type is represented by a dedicated token initialized from the contextualized EOS embedding of a degradation-oriented prompt and subsequently adapted during ultrasound SR training. A separate magnitude router predicts a continuous, input-dependent magnitude that modulates the corresponding token. Thus, language provides a degradation-aware initialization for what should be restored, while magnitude routing supplies an explicit signal for how strongly it should influence restoration. DAP-MR can be added to both one-step and multi-step diffusion super-resolution frameworks without changing their core structures. Our experiments--on synthetic datasets with both in-domain and under anatomical-domain shift, as well as unpaired real-world ultrasound data--show that DAP-MR delivers better restoration quality and generalizes more consistently across different domains.

title: Efficient Nominal Automata Computation with Strong Nominal Sets
authors: Hiroya Fujinami
abstract: Nominal automata and register automata are expressively equivalent models of computation over infinite alphabets, yet an algorithmic gap separates them in practice: dedicated algorithms decide language equivalence of deterministic register automata in polynomial time by working orbit-wise, while general-purpose nominal-computation tools that rely on SMT solvers hide the orbit structure and degrade rapidly even on small instances. We trace this gap to non-trivial local symmetries in nominal sets and observe that the configuration spaces of register automata correspond to strong nominal sets, whose elements carry only trivial local symmetries. We characterize strong nominal sets categorically, consolidating known and new equivalences, and derive a constraint-free array representation of orbit-finite strong nominal sets and equivariant maps; we further prove the existence of projective covers, guaranteeing that every nominal set admits a strong approximation preserving both orbit count and dimensions, computable for quotients of strong nominal sets. Building on these results, we develop concrete algorithms for language equivalence, minimization, and active learning, bridging the algorithmic gap for equivalence (in polynomial time for a fixed alphabet dimension) and extending the orbit-wise approach to minimization and learning. Finally, our implementation Namae, based on the array representation, outperforms existing nominal-computation tools and, at scale, stays within a small constant factor of a dedicated register-automaton equivalence tool.

title: Global strong solutions to isentropic compressible Navier--Stokes equations under a scaling-invariant smallness condition in $\mathbb{R}^2$
authors: Huanyao Wen, Jiayan Wu
abstract: In this paper, we consider the Cauchy problem for the isentropic compressible Navier--Stokes equations with vacuum at far field in two dimensions. Under an explicit scaling-invariant smallness condition on the initial data, we establish the global existence and uniqueness of strong solutions. The scaling-invariant smallness condition implies some classes of large data. The main difficulty is to obtain a uniform upper bound for the density under such the condition. Some new estimates of the dissipation and time-weighted energy estimates with explicit dependence on the initial data are derived, which control the effective viscous flux and close the a priori upper bound for density. In addition, we also obtain algebraic decay of the pressure and the velocity gradient.

title: Synchronized Normalized Solutions for a Critical Caffarelli--Kohn--Nirenberg System
authors: Shengbing Deng, Yifan Zhao
abstract: We study positive synchronized normalized solutions to the critical Caffarelli--Kohn--Nirenberg system: \begin{equation*} \left\{ \begin{aligned} -\operatorname{div}(|x|^{-2a}\nabla u) &=λ_1|x|^{-2a}u+β_1|x|^{-bq}|u|^{q-2}u &\quad+|x|^{-bp}\left( μ_1|u|^{p-2}u +να|u|^{α-2}u|v|^γ \right),\quad\text{in }\mathbb R^N, -\operatorname{div}(|x|^{-2a}\nabla v) &=λ_2|x|^{-2a}v+β_2|x|^{-bq}|v|^{q-2}v &\quad+|x|^{-bp}\left( μ_2|v|^{p-2}v +νγ|u|^α|v|^{γ-2}v \right),\quad\text{in }\mathbb R^N, \end{aligned} \right. \end{equation*} subject to the prescribed weighted masses \begin{equation*} \int_{\mathbb R^N}|x|^{-2a}u^2\,dx=ρ_1^2, \qquad \int_{\mathbb R^N}|x|^{-2a}v^2\,dx=ρ_2^2, \end{equation*} where $N\geq5$, $0\leq a<\frac{N-4}{2}$, $a<b<a+1$, $α,γ>1$, $α+γ=p=\frac{2N}{N-2(1+a-b)}$, $2<q<p$, $β_i,μ_i,ρ_i>0$ for $i=1,2$, and $ν>0$. The associated Lagrange multipliers $λ_1,λ_2\in\mathbb R$ are unknown. Under suitable algebraic compatibility conditions, we establish existence and multiplicity results for positive synchronized normalized solutions. The construction is based on synchronized reduction and critical energy estimates involving a finite-mass Caffarelli--Kohn--Nirenberg extremal. In the mass-subcritical regime, we find two positive solutions with opposite energies when $β=β_1ρ_1^{q-2}=β_2ρ_2^{q-2}$ is sufficiently small. In the mass-critical and mass-supercritical regimes, we obtain a synchronized Pohozaev ground state below the critical energy threshold for sufficiently small $β$ and for all $β>0$, respectively.

title: Breaking Visual Conventions: Spectrally Coupled Weight Perturbation for Creative Image Generation
authors: Fu Feng, Ruoheng Zhou, Yucheng Xie, Xu Yang, Jing Wang, Xin Geng
abstract: Text-to-image (T2I) models often produce high-quality images that follow familiar visual conventions, even in response to open-ended prompts such as ``a creative [CLS]''. Existing methods encourage novelty by exploring semantic conditions or modifying features and guidance during denoising. Pretrained weights offer a complementary source of creative variation, but unstructured perturbations can have little visual effect or degrade image quality. We introduce Coupled Spectral Perturbation (CosPert), a training-free method that targets attention projections in layers identified by a one-time sensitivity analysis. For each projection, CosPert uses a shared random transformation and its transpose to couple updates to the singular-vector factors while perturbing the spectral gains. A common relative budget calibrates the magnitude of weight changes across projections, and a sigmoid schedule concentrates their influence in early denoising and gradually attenuates them during refinement. CosPert provides plug-and-play creativity enhancement at inference time. Once the perturbations are prepared, sampling requires no auxiliary networks or additional model evaluations. On both FLUX.1 and Stable Diffusion 3.5, CosPert enhances visual creativity, producing more varied object structures while preserving category identity. Across 50 object categories, CosPert achieves the highest mean CREward among the evaluated methods while maintaining strong prompt alignment.

title: Stability of Homochiral Peptides in Capillary Environments: Implications for the Origin of Biological Homochirality
authors: Søren Toxvaerd
abstract: The homochiral proteins in living organisms are rather stable, but they tend to lose their secondary conformations and homochiral order over time. This instability is found in all living organisms, from bacteria to humans. The aging of living organisms, with the destruction of their vital homochiral order, raises the questions about the emergence of homochirality and how the homochiral order in the building molecules was ensured in prebiotic times before life evolved. Based on thermodynamic arguments, we propose that the homochiral order was achieved by a ``Frank-synthesis'' of homochiral peptides from racemic amino acids and in a capillary environment in the vents in the Earth's crust, perhaps at crystalline chiral surfaces, and that the peptides are stable over long times in such an environment. The $hypothesis$ can be confirmed by experimental analysis of the stability of the secondary structures in proteins as a function of water activity and in a capillary environment.

title: EviDARL: Evidence-Centric Dual-Agent Reasoning via Alternating Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Table Question Answering
authors: Dunhan Li, Leilei Gan, Lirong Gao, Wenyan Fan, Yongwei Wang, Sheng Guo, Fei Wu
abstract: Despite advances in LLM-based table reasoning, most studies focus on single-table settings. Multi-table QA requires multi-hop reasoning over complex table relationships and evidence dispersed across long contexts, often without verifiable intermediate traces. To address these challenges, we introduce EviDA, an evidence-centric dual-agent framework comprising an Evidence Construction Agent and a Reasoning and Answering Agent. The Evidence Construction Agent generates and executes table-manipulation programs over complete tables to produce question-specific evidence and verifiable intermediate traces, simplifying subsequent reasoning. The Reasoning and Answering Agent then performs multi-hop reasoning over this evidence to derive final answers. We further introduce EviDARL, which combines agent-specific fine-grained rewards with parameter-efficient alternating reinforcement learning to improve collaboration between the agents. By optimizing each agent in turn while holding the other fixed, EviDARL enables bidirectional adaptation between evidence construction and answer reasoning. Experiments on MMQA and TQA-Bench demonstrate that EviDARL substantially outperforms competitive open-model and multi-table reasoning baselines under constrained model and training budgets.

title: The Pólya-Szegő inequalities for polygons
authors: Hedong Wang
abstract: Of the simple polygons of given area with at most $n$ sides, $n\ge5$, the regular $n$-gon uniquely maximizes torsional rigidity and minimizes the first Dirichlet eigenvalue, up to congruence. The same polygon minimizes the Dirichlet Sobolev quotient for $1\le q\le2$. For convex polygons the proof uses mixed boundary problems on a partition. When there are fewer than $n$ convex vertices, the exterior angles give a lower bound on the torsion deficit. The torsion and eigenvalue inequalities have quadratic stability in Hausdorff distance at fixed area and at fixed perimeter, with optimal exponent.

title: Cross-Modal StateKV Injection for Communication in Multi-LLM Systems across Temporal Segments
authors: Xiaoqian Zhang, Zhihao Zhang
abstract: Video understanding with multiple multimodal language models requires a communication interface that can transfer complementary visual observations. Text-based communication is interpretable, but introduces an intermediate generation stage and can omit information relevant to subsequent reasoning. We study Cross-Modal StateKV Injection, a provider--carrier framework that communicates through key--value (KV) states at visual-token positions. Provider models observe complementary video frames; their visual KV states are aligned and projected into the carrier representation space and integrated through gated residual updates. Injection preserves the carrier KV-cache sequence length, while retaining the additional computation required by the providers and the communication module. The reported experiments on MLVU and Video-MME compare carrier-only inference, text-based communication, and StateKV with two provider architectures. Results show modest, task-dependent accuracy gains and lower reported latency than the evaluated text-communication baseline, with some categories remaining unchanged or decreasing. Increasing provider-side frame coverage offers additional gains on selected tasks without extending the carrier cache. These findings motivate further study of visual KV communication under explicitly controlled observation and computation budgets.

title: Where Do Human-to-Robot Transfer Gains Come From?
authors: Jiachen Li, Shihao Li, Soovadeep Bakshi, Longteng Fan, Dongmei Chen, Long Chen, Zhuo Xu
abstract: Human data can support robot policy pretraining, but gains attributed to a data recipe may also reflect subset size, training variability, or downstream adaptation. In an HPT implementation on a 20-task MetaWorld suite with three training blocks, a constrained random 5,000-recording subset matches most of the task-informed subset's gain over the 40,000-recording pool at 20,000 updates (3.69 of 4.29 percentage points), leaving equal-size selection differences of 0.60 points at 5,000 recordings and 0.45 points at 1,250 recordings, with wide paired intervals. Across 12 comparisons, task orderings repeat across seeds for several contrasts, but a fixed predictor built from the other two seeds trails the mean or difficulty reference in at least one held-out fold for every comparison. Neither mechanism probe shows its predicted positive interaction: task-slot mismatch yields an interaction of $-0.0347$ points after adaptation, and in a six-task observation experiment the observation-by-pretraining interaction changes sign between seeds ($-18.29$ and $+1.04$ points) while full-state pretraining gains are positive in both ($+6.37$ and $+2.31$ points). This retrospective study shows how equal-size and capacity controls, seed-level reporting, and targeted interventions change the interpretation of apparent transfer gains.

title: Streaming On-Policy Distillation: Decoupling Three Clocks for Stage-Wise Supervision Consumption
authors: Yun Zhu Da Wang
abstract: In on-policy distillation (OPD), response completion, supervision delivery, and parameter updates need not share the same granularity. We develop streaming OPD by decoupling these three clocks: a response repeatedly delivers newly generated segments while generation continues, retaining the full causal prefix at each delivery and computing loss only on new positions. A consumption protocol then organizes supervision budgets, position selection, staleness handling, and update scheduling, allowing control over quantity, coverage, and version lag across training stages. In GSM8K experiments distilling Qwen3-4B into Qwen3-0.6B with VERL, supervised-budget matching reduces the early gap between best test accuracies over seven common candidates from 4.55 to 2.42 points. Synchronous continuation from the same checkpoint reaches 73.39% best test accuracy over seven common candidates at u=384,...,576, versus 74.30% synchronous and 71.95% budget-matched (differences -0.91 and -2.35 points); an unpaired extended record reaches 76.12%. Freshness filtering and disagreement-overlap selection improve local peaks but do not establish sustained advantages. A system prototype shows lower data-supply waiting times without establishing an equal-update speedup. Quality recovery and supply-side benefits are assessed separately; end-to-end gains must account for continuation cost.

title: SpecSearch: Towards Hardware-Aware Efficient Speculative Decoding
authors: Selin Yildirim, Ali Zeyrek, Deming Chen
abstract: Speculative decoding (SD) accelerates large language model (LLM) inference, but its optimal configuration depends jointly on workload characteristics, GPU hardware, and available memory. For example, on the RTX~5090, the state-of-the-art speculative drafter DFlash achieves $3.50\times$ the throughput of autoregressive (AR) decoding at low concurrency, but only $0.76\times$ at high concurrency with short outputs. We present SpecSearch, a hardware-aware search engine that jointly optimizes decoding strategy, draft length, and precision across workload--GPU pairs. Its analytical cost model captures memory and compute constraints to identify feasible configurations and narrow the search space for throughput optimization. Guided by this model, calibration measurements are collected from multiple GPUs. Using the measurements, a Jev-based predictor learns to select high-throughput decoding configurations on held-out GPUs without requiring deployment-GPU calibration. The predictor is parameter-efficiently trained on calibration data, while adapting a frozen Qwen3-4B using LoRA adapters and a linear correction layer. Across NVIDIA RTX~5090, H100, L40 and AMD MI300X GPUs, SpecSearch with full calibration achieves an average of $2.01\times$ the throughput of AR and $1.36\times$ the throughput of SD, both served by vLLM. The proposed Jev-based predictor closely matches this search performance with $1.30\times$ throughput improvement over SD with vLLM, while eliminating the need for held-out GPU calibration. Additionally, it retains $97.36\%$ of the throughput achieved by SpecSearch that utilizes full calibration.

title: Learning Regions of Attraction for Transverse Feedback Linearization under Controller Singularities
authors: Abdullah Waqar Malik, Hamza Tariq, Adeel Akhtar
abstract: Transverse feedback linearization (TFL) achieves path following by exactly linearizing the error dynamics, but its controller is undefined on a singular set, such as zero speed for a unicycle or zero thrust for a quadrotor. The constrained region of attraction, the set of initial states from which the closed loop converges to the path without violating state or regularity constraints, determines where the controller can be safely activated. Exploiting the exact linear error dynamics, we show that this region is the largest forward invariant subset of the admissible set. We then decompose its state-constrained Zubov value function into an analytically known quadratic cost-to-go and a safety value function. We learn only the latter, by fitted value iteration without infinite-horizon trajectory labels. The resulting estimate combines an inner layer verified by interval branch and bound with a learned outer layer tested on samples. On a unicycle following a circle and a sinusoid and on a planar quadrotor, it covers on average 72.0%, 83.4% and 19.1% of the simulated region of attraction. In comparison, the quadratic cost-to-go and two physics-informed neural network (PINN) solvers of Zubov's equation cover at most 11.3%, 4.0% and 0.0% on average. Code and animations are available at https://gradslab.github.io/roa_tfl

title: Uniform spatial Schauder estimates for backward stochastic partial differential equations with random coefficients
authors: Yunzhang Li, Shanjian Tang, Yuyang Ye
abstract: We prove spatial Schauder estimates for super-parabolic backward stochastic partial differential equations. All coefficients can be random and depend on time and space, and the estimates are uniform in probability and time. The key ingredient is a weighted conditional energy norm adapted to the parabolic scale of each frequency block. Together with heat-kernel bounds and coefficient freezing, it controls the gradient-martingale coupling without assuming a bounded martingale integrand. As an application, we establish Schauder solvability for semilinear stochastic Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman equations.

title: Nonlocal regularization of sharp-crack energetics: a variational bridge from Griffith geometry to emergent constitutive degradation
authors: Qing Cheng, Yuqi Sun, Xuejun Xu
abstract: We develop a variational diffuse-crack model based on nonlocal averaging of tensile strain energy. A bounded potential acts on the scaled average, while the compressive energy remains local. The initial slope preserves the averaged tensile strain-energy density to leading order. The first variation yields a constitutive stress in which the tensile contribution is multiplied by the adjoint average of the derivative of the saturation potential. The resulting degradation is therefore determined by the stored-energy functional, without introducing an independent fracture field or prescribing a separate degradation law. For fixed smooth displacement fields with bounded strain, the energy density converges to the classical elastic strain-energy density as the averaging radius tends to zero. The Griffith surface-energy coefficient is recovered for planar opening transitions. A structure-preserving scalar auxiliary variable (SAV) scheme satisfies an exact discrete balance between the modified-energy increment and external work. We compare SAV and velocity-Verlet solutions for dynamic crack branching and Kalthoff--Winkler impact.

title: SeasonRainBench: Global Seasonal Precipitation
authors: Qiuyan Sun, Mengxuan Chen, Haoyuan Liang, Guowen Li, Zhen Huang, Jianhao Lin, Juepeng Zheng, Haohuan Fu
abstract: Accurate seasonal precipitation forecasts help societies prepare for drought, flooding, and crop failure months in advance. While data-driven methods have made rapid progress in weather and subseasonal forecasting, operational seasonal precipitation prediction still relies on numerical ensemble systems. These systems are computationally expensive and exhibit biases and drift that increase with lead time, motivating more efficient data-driven alternatives. Yet this transition faces three linked challenges: comparing data-driven forecasts with operational ones requires (1) a global benchmark that does not exist, scoring them requires (2) metrics that capture operational priorities beyond anomaly correlation (ACC) and RMSE, and training them must (3) rely on a single, short observational record. To address the first two challenges, we introduce \BenchName, the first such benchmark, covering monthly precipitation forecasts 1--5 months ahead. It pairs global $1^\circ$ satellite precipitation with oceanic and atmospheric predictors, includes seven operational centers, and provides 310,944 simulated months from 52 climate models for training. Beyond standard scores, we introduce two operationally motivated metrics for anomaly strength and monthly rain-belt position. To address the third challenge, we develop \MODEL, which learns from simulations what the record lacks and transfers it to Earth through three modules: SimForced aligns the climate background, SimMemory transfers a history encoder pretrained on simulations, and SimAnalog supplements Earth labels with simulated analog outcomes. Extensive experiments show that \MODEL{} improves ACC, CRPS, anomaly strength, and rain-belt position by 12.0\%, 3.6\%, 2.9\%, and 0.3\% over the strongest operational or data-driven model, opening a path from simulated worlds to Earth system prediction.

title: Doing Well by Doing Good: Alignment of Revenue and Welfare in Robust Product Line Design through Data-Driven Optimization
authors: Maoqi Liu, Liangjie Li, Yun Hui Lin, Xiuli Chao, Jiajie Zhang
abstract: Product line design (PLD) selects product variants for a firm to maximize expected revenue. Candidate assortments are usually evaluated under random utility maximization (RUM), in which choice probabilities stem from the joint distribution of latent consumer utilities. As this utility distribution cannot be directly observed and is estimated from choice data, distributional uncertainty inevitably arises. This paper studies how to hedge PLD decisions against such ambiguity. We construct a distributionally robust optimization (DRO) model that maximizes worst-case expected revenue over an l1-Wasserstein ball around a nominal utility distribution. We derive a dual reformulation for general nominal distributions and then specialize to two cases. With independent Gumbel utility shocks, the dual simplifies to a closed-form robust multinomial logit. We derive revenue gap bounds for parameters estimated from finite full-assortment choice data. When the true model structure is unknown beforehand, we adopt a data-driven scheme using the empirical distribution of sampled utility vectors and extend optimality-gap analysis to a general RUM oracle. For the NP-hard empirical problem, we propose Adaptive Parametric Search (APS), an algorithm with certified relative optimality guarantees. Numerical experiments show fast computation and better out-of-sample performance.Dual analysis shows that robustness to preference uncertainty endogenously encourages the firm to raise buyer welfare. This incentive takes distinct forms: robustness supports larger assortments in the unconstrained logit setting, whereas under the empirical nominal, it favors products with lower prices and higher utility relative to the outside option. Numerically, we identify a "doing well by doing good" effect: product lines with higher in-sample buyer welfare attain higher out-of-sample revenue and buyer welfare.

title: Multi-Gaussian Model for Intrabeam Scattering
authors: Wenxuan Wu, Zhilong Pan, Chuanxiang Tang, Xiujie Deng
abstract: Conventional analytical models of intrabeam scattering (IBS), such as the Piwinski model and Bjorken-Mtingwa model, generally rely on the assumption of a Gaussian beam distribution, limiting their applicability to non-Gaussian cases. In this work, we develop a multi-Gaussian model to extend analytical IBS calculations to a broader class of non-Gaussian phase-space distributions. The proposed approach represents a non-Gaussian distribution as a superposition of Gaussian components sharing a common covariance matrix but having different mean values. We derived a generalized model for evaluating the momentum second-moment evolution rate and the IBS growth rate. Furthermore, for equally spaced Gaussian components, we developed an infinite bunch train model and introduce a practical truncation rule to reduce computational costs. The model is applied to a representative steady-state microbunching (SSMB) storage ring, where longitudinal overlap between neighboring microbunches is shown to enhance IBS growth rates in all three directions. The proposed framework provides a practical approach to evaluating IBS in non-Gaussian beam distributions and offers a basis for further development toward a more general non-Gaussian IBS theory.

title: Recovering hysteresis in reduced models of plasma turbulence: a Mori--Zwanzig-inspired closure
authors: Ameir Shaa, Kyungtak Lim, Claude Guet, Xavier Garbet
abstract: Hysteretic transitions between turbulent and strongly zonal-flow-dominated states provide an important test for reduced models of plasma turbulence and a minimal setting for studying dynamics relevant to L-H transitions. The 12-mode truncation of the modified Hasegawa-Wakatani system developed by Guillon and Gürcan retains this transition but underestimates the hysteresis observed in direct numerical simulations (DNS). Guided by the Mori-Zwanzig framework, we construct a phenomenological closure for the influence of discarded modes. The discarded spectrum is coarse-grained into a reservoir, whose feedback on the retained modes is modeled together with a separate drift-wave damping term. Without increasing the number of retained modes, the closure recovers nearly all of the hysteresis width missing from the unclosed truncation and places both transition thresholds close to their DNS values. To test the model beyond hysteresis, we also examine particle flux. The closed model improves upon the unclosed truncation, agreeing more closely with DNS at low adiabaticity but underestimating transport at high adiabaticity. These results show that a low-dimensional representation of discarded-mode feedback can improve predictions of hysteretic turbulence-flow transitions.

title: Multispectral-Polarization-Infrared Multi-Aperture Camouflaged Vehicle Detection
authors: Shu Wang, Xiong Lin, Yuan Song, Junjie Wang, Feng Huang, Wenxi Liu
abstract: Camouflaged vehicle detection is challenging because camouflage suppresses discriminative cues across sensing modalities. Existing multimodal methods often require precise pixel-level registration and feature-level fusion, creating a trade-off between accuracy and latency. We propose a spectral-polarization-infrared tri-modal detection framework co-designed with a multi-aperture imaging setup to exploit complementary imaging physics. A consensus-guided decision-level fusion strategy combines cross-modal detections within bounded registration tolerances, reducing dependence on precise alignment while maintaining accuracy and real-time performance. We construct a tri-modal camouflaged vehicle dataset containing infrared, polarization, and spectral data. Experiments show that the proposed method achieves 82.7% mean Average Precision (mAP) with an end-to-end latency of 16 ms, outperforming representative feature-level fusion approaches. On the public MID-1K dataset, the framework generalizes to RGB-Depth-Infrared modalities without architectural modification and improves mAP@0.5 by 5.7% over state-of-the-art methods. These results demonstrate the potential of decision-level consensus fusion and multi-aperture sensing for robust and deployable camouflaged vehicle detection.

title: PhyVGGT: Feed-Forward Articulated Object Reconstruction from Monocular Videos
authors: Qi Shao, Zhihao Cao, Shuhao Zhai, Anh Nguyen, Hong Liang, Baoru Huang, Liang Li
abstract: Reconstructing an articulated object with its 3D movable parts, joint parameters and unseen articulation states from an uncalibrated monocular video is essential for robot manipulation and interactive digital twins. Existing per-scene optimisation methods require minutes to hours and external depth or camera poses, whereas feed-forward 3D foundation models reconstruct dense point maps in one pass without segmenting movable parts or inferring joints. Even on these monocular point maps, regressing or fitting continuous joints directly fails on casual videos, since cross-frame attention blurs moving part boundaries in deep layers, underestimates motion along the viewing ray and leaves continuous axes ill-conditioned under small opening angles. To address these challenges, we propose PhyVGGT, a single-pass framework on a frozen 3D foundation model that anchors moving-part matching and closed-form joint estimation to the undistorted geometry of the stationary base. First, our Part and Motion Decoder fuses intermediate per-frame tokens with global tokens and references part queries to a static-base query to segment 3D parts, align point maps on the static base and predict learned Bingham priors. Second, our Kinematic Inference Layer fits an orthogonal Manhattan frame to static surface normals, selects the joint axis in closed form under a Bingham posterior combining pairwise motion scatter with the learned priors, and solves a linear system for the hinge pivot to drive unseen states. Trained solely on synthetic data, PhyVGGT achieves state-of-the-art monocular performance across five benchmarks, outperforming FAMOS and monocular ArtiPoint, surpassing posed RGB-D ArtiPoint in median error, and running in 6.8 s per 48-frame video against hours of per-scene optimisation in Articulat3D. Project page: https://phyvggt.github.io.

title: From Token Changes to Task Failures: Bit Flips in a Shared KV-Cache Block
authors: Yuji Yamamoto, Satoshi Matsuura
abstract: In LLM serving systems with prefix caching, each KV block of a shared system prompt is held in GPU memory as a single physical copy, which every request with that prompt reads. Our earlier work measured change and showed that one bit flip in such a block changes many later responses without making them visibly degenerate. This paper extends that work by measuring how often the changed responses are wrong. Using software fault injection into vLLM serving Qwen3-8B, we flip the most significant mantissa bit or the sign bit of a value in such a block. We score responses on four tasks: code generation, short-answer questions, multiple-choice reasoning, and refusal under a policy. The fraction of changes that turned a correct response wrong depended strongly on the task: 0.023 on MBPP+ and 0.59 on held-out TriviaQA at the mantissa bit, and 0.019 and 0.60 at the sign bit. Harm fell on requests whose sampled answers are sometimes wrong, so the damage of a flip depends on how common such requests are. Harmed responses looked like ordinary errors, so a flip should be detected by checking cached blocks rather than by monitoring outputs.

title: Context Has a Price: Adding and Removing Context for LLM Coding Agents under Prefix Caching
authors: Zerui Yang, Miaomiao Dong, Quan Xue, Chaorui Zhang, Xuanyu Zheng, Xiyuan Wang, Haolin Ruan, Xueyan Niu, Guangcheng Song, Weixi Zhang, Wei Han, Bo Bai
abstract: Coding agents repeatedly send their conversation history to a language model. Adding useful code may reduce search, while removing old tool outputs may shorten later prompts. But do these changes reduce the cost of solving a task? We study this as a measurement problem in more than 20,000 runs of open models on SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench and Loc-Bench. We account separately for uncached input, cached input and output tokens. Three findings emerge. First, in our main evidence-package experiments, retrieved code reduces read and search commands by 18--34%, but increases cost by 33--42% when cached input costs one tenth of uncached input, without a measurable improvement in resolution. Second, removing old observations can either save money or increase cost: the same approach saves 19--36% without a cache discount but increases cost by 38--116% with a tenth-price cache. Third, shorter prompts do not guarantee cheaper runs because agents may respond by taking more steps. We also find that concurrent experiments can share cached prefixes and distort cost comparisons. These results show why context-management methods should be evaluated using both token prices and the agent's subsequent behavior.

title: Flavor Entanglement as a CPT Violation Witness in Neutrino Oscillations
authors: Bipin Singh Koranga, Biswmkwr Boro, Vivek Kumar Nautiyal
abstract: We present a comprehensive study linking the single-particle flavor entanglement of a \(ν_{e} \rightarrow ν_μ\) oscillation to CPT violation using the concurrence.
