In the absence of fault-tolerant machines, ensemble learning, which combines multiple imperfect quantum devices, may unlock new quantum computing applications. Here, we introduce two ensemble-learning algorithms, namely Bagging and AdaBoost, for enhancing the accuracy of nonlinear regression problems. While Bagging trains variational quantum regressors independently, AdaBoost employs a sequential training strategy and achieves significantly better prediction accuracy. By incorporating systematic feature selection into our ensemble learning algorithms, we enhance their predictive power for highly nonlinear functions. We further improve prediction accuracy through a feature-to-qubit mapping strategy based on repeated feature encoding. The performance of our ensemble-based algorithms improves with both the number of regressors in the ensemble and the size of each regressor. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach using four benchmarking functions with varying degrees of nonlinearity by relying on a feature pool limited to first- and second-order polynomial terms.

title: DGV-DLIVO: Degeneracy-Guided Visual Fusion for Direct LiDAR-Inertial-Visual Odometry in Degenerate Tunnel Environments
authors: Junrui Zhang
abstract: Reliable localization in long underground infrastructures remains a major challenge for autonomous inspection robots. In hydropower spillway tunnels and drainage galleries, repetitive geometric structures provide insufficient constraints along the tunnel axis, while weak texture and illumination variations further degrade visual estimation. Under this coupled degradation, existing LiDAR-inertial and visual-inertial odometry systems may lose the ability to recover continuous longitudinal motion. This paper presents DGV-DLIVO, a degeneracy-guided visual fusion for direct LiDAR-inertial-visual odometry for extreme tunnel environments. Instead of treating vision as a general complementary sensor, the proposed method exploits the LiDAR-degenerate direction as an active guidance signal to determine informative visual regions, establish LiDAR-anchored visual associations, and perform subspace-selective fusion. The visual constraints are introduced only into the deficient motion subspace, while unreliable LiDAR information in the same direction is adaptively suppressed and reliable geometric constraints are preserved. Real-world experiments in hydropower tunnels demonstrate that representative state-of-the-art LIO, LIVO, and VIO methods suffer from stagnation, oscillation, severe under-travel, curved drift, or divergence, whereas DGV-DLIVO maintains continuous and directionally consistent tunnel-axis motion estimation under both cart-mounted and handheld acquisition. It achieves a 91.4% progress ratio over the 40m tunnel sequence and significantly improves longitudinal recovery and trajectory stability. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of degeneracy-guided adaptive fusion for robotic inspection in severely degraded underground environments. The source code and a supplementary video are publicly available at https://github.com/0RayZhang0/DGV-DLIVO.

title: Finite-Smoothing Efficiency and Inference in Single-Index Models
authors: Jiayang Xu, Yusen Jia, Yangzhou Chen, Xin Chen
abstract: When the error is independent of the predictors, its distribution can carry information about a single-index direction beyond the conditional mean. We develop Single-Index Kernel Density Regression (SI-KDR): at each candidate direction, it refits the link and evaluates a leave-one-out kernel log-likelihood of the residuals. Under Gaussian design, the population score vanishes at the true line at every positive smoothing tuple. At a fixed positive-curvature tuple, the leading covariance in the sample expansion is the conditional-mean efficiency bound times $Λ/G$, where $G$ is the information gain from independence and $Λ$ is the variance inflation from smoothing. We derive $Λ$ by following each observation through link refitting, the dual role of its residual as evaluation point and kernel center, and training standardization. Case-weight covariance estimates guide tuning for point estimation. Tuning separately at each candidate gives an exact conditional $F$ test. When predictors outnumber observations, independent screening that retains the support preserves the covariance comparison and the exact test, and $G/Λ$ becomes the squared-noncentrality ratio of a retained-coordinate test relative to the conditional-mean oracle. In four non-Gaussian error distribution designs at $n=600$, covariance-trace tuning reduced direction risk by 56% to 74% relative to reference bandwidths, and score-inversion coverage was 93.8% to 96.6%.

title: Global well-posedness and regularization for a nonlinear relativistic Fokker--Planck equation
authors: Simone Calogero
abstract: We consider a nonlinear relativistic Fokker--Planck equation on momentum space, whose diffusion coefficient and drift vector field are nonlinear integral functionals of the solution. We prove global existence and uniqueness of weak probability density solutions preserving the relativistic energy-momentum $(E,P)$. A fundamental step in the proof is to establish that the scalar diffusion coefficient remains uniformly positive on every finite time interval. The key mechanism ensuring this property is the strict relativistic inequality $E^2-|P|^2>1$, combined with the uniform integrability of the energy tails on every finite time interval. We further prove that global weak solutions become instantaneously smooth and strictly positive for positive times. Finally, for even initial data, we prove that the diffusion coefficient remains uniformly positive for all time.

title: Spectropolarimetric diagnostics of the lower solar atmosphere: a review of inversion techniques
authors: Ivan Milic
abstract: The Sun, our host star, plays a fundamental role in astrophysics due to its vicinity. To understand the processes taking place in the outermost layers of the Sun, but also, indirectly, in its interior, we conduct high spectral and spatial resolution, high cadence observations of diagnostically important spectral lines. The intensity and the polarization of the electromagnetic radiation in the observed spectral lines are a result of the joint action of absorption, emission, and scattering processes, further altered by the Zeeman and Hanle effects. Spectropolarimetric inversions are the techniques devised for the inference of the physical parameters in the solar atmosphere through the interpretation of spectral line shapes and line polarization. This review aims to provide a pedagogical overview of the necessary radiative transfer formalism and cutting-edge techniques, and to help interested readers enter the field and use some of the concepts in their own research. The secondary aim is a critical assessment of the emerging directions for the development of spectropolarimetric inversions, namely, to discuss the friction between physical realism, numerical efficiency, and modeling of the instrumental effects.

title: Resolving Individual Massive Stars in an M31 Star Cluster Exhibiting Wolf-Rayet Features
authors: Yunning Zhao, Yulong Gao, Wei Zhang, Fuzhen Cheng, Ming Yang, Shiming Wen, Shichao Han, Hong Wu
abstract: The observed ratio of Wolf-Rayet (WR) star subtypes (e.g., WC/WN) in M31 is significantly higher than the predictions of standard stellar evolution models, yet this key diagnostic discrepancy remains unresolved. This is partly due to incomplete census and the challenge of resolving individual stars in compact clusters with ground-based telescopes. In this work, we report a young cluster with WR features with the (R.A., Dec) = (00:43:39.36, +41:10:08.7), discovered with LAMOST spectra. We use the high spatial resolution of the HST imaging data to resolve the cluster members, leading to the identification of four WR star candidates, four OB stars, and one yellow supergiant. Based on the current known WR sample in M31 observed in the HST F275W filter, about one-third of WRs are contaminated by other sources within a 1. "1 $\times$ 1. "1 aperture, while this fraction can reach up to two-thirds for the LAMOST fiber size of 3. "3. Applying the approach demonstrated in this work to a larger sample of crowded regions in M31 will yield a more complete census and allow for the measurement of a definitive WC/WN ratio, corrected for contamination. Whether this refined ratio increases or decreases the current tension with models remains to be seen, but it will provide the essential observational constraint needed to advance our understanding.

title: Accounts on Synthetic Cells
authors: The Frontiers of Life Research Network, Sébastien Lecommandoux, Hamid Kellay, C. Axel Innis, Carole Lartigue, Joelle Amédée, Rosanna Le Scouarnec, Léonie Beaupère, Kevin Peyraud-Vicré, Paramita Chaudhuri, Seamoon Deb, Jitra-Marie Jittasevi, Chloé Manseau, Eloise Equy, Colin Bonduelle, Emmanuel Ibarboure, Elisabeth Garanger, Thomas Salez, Vandana Sharma, Antoine Aubret, Ulysse Delabre, Valérie Desvergnes, Jeanne Leblond Chain, Mikayel Aznauryan, Stéphane Arbault, Antoine Loquet, Yann Fichou, Anne Devin, Patrick Paumard, Sven J. Saupe, Amine Maarouf, Damien Coudreuse, Vivien Willems, Zi Lin, Eleni Kopsini, Esra Baydar, Jose Fojo, Emmanuel Joseph, Cristian Villalobos-Concha, Laura Alvarez, Jacques Leng, Thomas Beneyton, Etienne Ducrot, Aurore Dupin, Nicolas Martin, Hugo De Oliveira, Harald Wodrich, Bastien Lambert, Laure Beven, Pierre Nassoy, Jean-Christophe Baret
abstract: Frontiers of Life is a research network of the University of Bordeaux focused on the re-engineering of living systems, starting from the construction of a synthetic cell. In this article, we present our motivation to build a cell from scratch and the elementary building blocks we worked on over the past four years. While the final objective regarding the construction of a synthetic cell remains a long-term target, the reconstruction of living cells provides both a methodology and experimental approaches to improve our understanding of living systems with potential to become the next generation of biotechnologies.

title: An Inexact Proximal Gradient Method for Composite Multiobjective Optimization with Absolute and Relative Stopping Criteria
authors: Zhuoxin Fan, Liping Tang, Xinmin Yang
abstract: Proximal gradient methods are widely used for composite optimization. In multiobjective optimization, however, the resulting minimax subproblem generally requires an additional inner method to solve, even when the proximal mapping of each nonsmooth component is available in closed form. In addition, most existing convergence results are obtained only under the assumption that the involved subproblems are solved exactly, which is unrealistic and limits the applicability of the proximal gradient methods. To make the proximal gradient methods practical, we propose an implementable inexact proximal gradient method based on proximal computation. Considering an approximate optimality condition and a hybrid stopping criterion including absolute and relative rules for the subproblem, we address the computational challenge by developing an inner inexact projected gradient method that can exploit the proximal mappings of the individual components. The $\mathcal{O}(1/k)$ convergence rate is also established for our method under certain conditions. Numerical experiments illustrate the computational benefits of solving the subproblems inexactly.

title: Gradient estimate for $p$-heat equation on complete Riemannian manifold
authors: Weihao Zheng
abstract: We derive a Hamilton-type gradient estimate for positive solutions to the $p$-heat equation via the Moser iteration method. Our result relaxes the curvature assumption from sectional curvature to Ricci curvature. In addition, we obtain a Liouville-type theorem and a Harnack-type inequality as corollaries.

title: An AI-Driven Assistant for Human-Centric Building Digital Twin Systems: Design, Implementation, and Comparative User Evaluation
authors: Leonardo Messi, Erika Anneli Pärn, Juan Diego Castaño Molina, Oleksandr Anyshchenko, Dijar Selami, Peihang Luo, Borja García de Soto
abstract: Smart buildings generate streams of operational data, yet this richness rarely translates into accessible, decision-ready information for stakeholders who inhabit and manage them. Current Building Digital Twin Systems (BDTS) often remain oriented toward technical specialists and rely on static, one-size-fits-all interfaces. This paper presents the design, implementation, and comparative user evaluation of an AI-driven conversational assistant integrated into a human-centric BDTS for Indoor Environmental Quality monitoring, combined with adaptive information presentation and auto-suggest functionality. The prototype was deployed at New York University Abu Dhabi. A controlled, two-arm, between-subjects, quasi-experimental study with wave-based, non-randomized assignment compared the Baseline interface with the Experimental interface. Results showed significant reductions in task-completion time and perceived workload, while accuracy and usability improved but did not meet the adjusted significance criterion. The study contributes an implemented and empirically evaluated architecture that separates generative interaction from deterministic environmental assessment and coordinates conversational responses with adaptive visual presentation.

title: Dual-Comb Spectrometry Enabled by Gain-Assisted Electro-Optic Fiber Ring Resonators
authors: Yuan Chen, Jieming Zhang, Zijian Wang, Jia Xu, Mei Yang, Wending Huang, Rui Zhu, Zhen Hu, Xiangze Ma, Xiuxiu Zhang, Cong Jiang, Zhaoyang Wen, Zhuoren Wan, Ming Yan, Heping Zeng
abstract: Broadband dual-comb spectroscopy (DCS) with widely tunable repetition rates and simplified frequency stabilization is desirable for diverse sensing applications. Here, we demonstrate DCS using two gain-assisted fiber ring resonators that share a continuous-wave (CW) laser and incorporate intracavity electro-optic (EO) phase modulation. Intracavity gain compensates for round-trip losses, sustaining repeated phase modulation and enabling flat-top comb spectra with a 20-dB bandwidth exceeding 1.8 THz. Harmonic-order selection provides widely tunable repetition rates from approximately 5 to 0.2 GHz without substantially compromising the spectral bandwidth. The comb phase noise closely follows that of the radio-frequency (RF) drive at low offset frequencies. Without active frequency stabilization, the two combs exhibit an instrument-limited beat-note linewidth of 2 Hz, indicating high mutual coherence. The generated dual combs enable high-speed DCS at the single-interferogram rate, providing a platform for dynamic spectroscopic measurements. This all-fiber architecture, together with its simplified operation, offers a promising route towards compact and readily integrable dual-comb instruments.

title: TetherMark: Instance-Level Watermark Authentication Against Cross-Instance Transplantation
authors: Jin Wei, Rundong Li, Li Ma, Yikai Wang, Ruihao Yang, Jianxiong Wu, Xiaoyuan Duan, Yanbo Wang, Runyu Mao, Chen Fang, Chang Xu, Ping Chen, Jun Dai, Xiaoyan Sun
abstract: Robust watermarking is commonly verified by asking whether a hidden payload remains decodable after compression, geometric distortion, or generative editing. Localized and semantic extensions may additionally check whether an expected region or category is still present. These tests establish evidence validity or content consistency, but not whether the evidence still belongs to the particular visual instance registered by its owner. We expose cross-instance transplantation: an attacker extracts or estimates valid watermark evidence from one registered image and transfers it to a different image of the same category. The message can still decode, the expected content can remain present, and the result can look natural, even though the evidence has been reassigned to the wrong instance. To enable instance-level watermark authentication, we introduce TetherMark, a post-hoc watermark that combines two complementary checks. The message check verifies an edit-robust payload, while the relation check uses secret patch-pair selection, a registered response, natural correspondence transport, and enrollment normalization to test consistency with the registered instance. The verifier accepts only when both checks pass. Across 240 test subjects, TetherMark attains 92.08% legitimate true acceptance with 9.17% and 16.25% attack success under WmForger and WMCopier, respectively, yielding the highest instance-binding balanced accuracy under both attacks.

title: iBraid group symmetries of iquantum groups via star product
authors: Ming Lu, Xujie Zhou
abstract: We establish ibraid group symmetries on universal iquantum groups of symmetrizable Kac-Moody type, proving a conjecture of Wang and Zhang. Building on the star product realization of quantum symmetric pairs $(\widetilde{\mathbf U},\widetilde{\mathbf U}^{\imath})$, we relate these symmetries to Lusztig's braid group symmetries, extending the compatibility previously obtained via iHopf algebras in the quasi-split setting. Via the Letzter map $ψ$ from the iquantum group $\widetilde{\mathbf U}^{\imath}$ to the horospherical algebra $\mathcal A\subset \widetilde{\mathbf U}$, we show that the ibraid group symmetry $\widetilde{\mathbf T}'_{i,-1}$ of $\widetilde{\mathbf U}^{\imath}$ transported to $\mathcal A$ coincides with Lusztig's braid group symmetry $\widetilde T_{\mathbf r_i}^{-1}$ on the subalgebra $\mathcal R_{\bullet,i}^{-,r}$. Finally, a mixed product formula, together with a parabolic decomposition, yields an explicit formula for the transported action on the entire horospherical algebra $\mathcal A$.

title: Comparing Implicit and Explicit Language Attitudes toward the Dutch multiethnolect Straattaal in Humans and Large Language Models
authors: Hedwig Oldenhof, Laura Rosseel, Anna Wegmann, Dong Nguyen
abstract: While language attitudes have been extensively studied in humans, the extent to which large language models (LLMs) encode similar associations between language varieties and social attributes remains unclear. Contemporary sociolinguistic research distinguishes between explicit attitudes, which stem from deliberative processing, and implicit attitudes, which arise from automatic processing. This study investigates whether LLMs exhibit human-like implicit and explicit language attitudes toward the Dutch multiethnolect Straattaal, particularly its association with migrant communities. We use closely matched designs to assess attitudes in humans and LLMs. For humans, we use an Implicit Association Test (IAT) and an explicit rating task. For LLMs, we use the LLM Word Association Test (LLM WAT) and the same explicit rating task. Human participants strongly associate Straattaal with individuals with a migration background at both implicit and explicit levels. In the LLM WAT, Straattaal is consistently associated with individuals with a migration background, with stronger associations observed in larger and newer models. When presented with the same explicit rating task as human participants, LLMs produce comparable response patterns. Overall, the findings suggest that many LLMs encode language attitudes resembling those observed in humans, however we also highlight important questions about how concepts and measures developed to study human attitudes should be interpreted in LLMs. This highlights the relevance of incorporating sociolinguistic perspectives and language variation into NLP research to better identify and mitigate socially and linguistically embedded biases.

title: BQ-LoRA: Binary-Quantized Low-Rank Adapters as Implicit Regularizers for Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning
authors: Juyoung Park, Heejun Lee
abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning of quantized large language models is dominated by QLoRA, which combines 4-bit weight quantization with FP16 low-rank adapters. We ask whether the FP16 adapter precision is necessary. Replacing it with a single binary bit per adapter parameter, combined with a learned per-layer scale $s$ and a Scaled Straight-Through Estimator, reduces adapter storage by 13-16x. We introduce two variants -- NormScale, which binarizes under a norm-preserving scale with a clipped STE, and LearnThresh, which makes the binarization threshold learnable -- unified under a framework we call BQ-LoRA. Our main theoretical contribution is a tight characterization of the BQ-LoRA hypothesis class: it has bounded entrywise norm, a typical-set spectral norm bound that is $Θ(r)$ times sharper than the worst case, a full-rank, near-isotropic update, and consequently a Rademacher complexity that yields an explicit $\tilde{O}(s_{\max}α\sqrt{d_{out}/(rn)})$ generalization bound. FP16 LoRA has no comparable a priori norm or isotropy control. On Qwen2.5 (1.5B-72B), BQ-LoRA exceeds QLoRA's benchmark averages at every scale by 0.8-3.5 points; on LLaMA-2 (7B/70B) it remains competitive at the same storage reduction but does not uniformly lead the strongest FP16-adapter baselines (LoftQ at 7B, QLoRA at 70B). On Qwen2.5-7B the binary adapter preserves the 4-bit base WikiText-2 PPL within 0.06 (9.86 vs. 9.80) while QLoRA worsens it by 0.59. The reduction applies to inference-time adapter storage and serving; training memory matches QLoRA and step time rises by under 4%. We translate the storage saving into a deployment study, BQ-SGMV, by extending Punica's SGMV kernel with a binary inner-product primitive: the same A100-80GB holds 15.6x more adapters in HBM, and our research prototype eliminates cache misses under a skewed synthetic workload.

title: Gradient Ascent Pulse Engineering for Multi-Time Correlations
authors: Issei Matsuzoe, Kazufumi Tanji, Wojciech Roga, Masahiro Takeoka
abstract: In quantum optimal control, gradient methods are often used to optimize functions of a state or propagator at a final time, while experimentally addressable observables and performance metrics may depend on multi-time correlations. We develop QRT-GRAPE, which combines the quantum regression theorem (QRT) with Gradient Ascent Pulse Engineering (GRAPE) to obtain analytic gradients for objective functions defined by multi-time correlations. The method incorporates the time evolution of an auxiliary operator in QRT into the forward propagation and backward adjoint propagation used in GRAPE. As an application, we consider the trade-off between the photon-emission probability and the conditional Bell-state fidelity in heralded remote entanglement generation among two nonidentical atom--cavity systems. Starting from a flat-top Rabi pulse pair selected by a search over pulse amplitudes and durations, QRT-GRAPE increases the photon-emission probability product from $0.2802$ to $0.3216$ and the conditional Bell-state fidelity from $0.9356$ to $0.9441$.

title: Global Well-Posedness of Two-Dimensional Compressible Navier--Stokes Equations with Vacuum under a Scaling-Invariant Smallness Condition
authors: Boqiang Lü, Xin Song
abstract: In this paper, we consider the Cauchy problem for the two-dimensional isentropic compressible Navier--Stokes equations with vacuum as far-field density. For the initial data that satisfy suitable regularity conditions, we establish the global well-posedness of strong solutions, provided that the scaling-invariant initial quantity \( \barρ \big( \|ρ_0\|_{L^1} + \barρ^{-2γ} \|ρ_0\|_{L^1}^{-1} + \barρ^{\frac{α(γ+1)}{2}} \|ρ_0 |x|^α\|_{L^1} \big) (1+\barρ E_0)^{3/2} \big( \|\nabla u_0\|_{L^2}^2 + \|ρ_0^γ\|_{L^2}^2 \big) \) is sufficiently small. Moreover, if the initial data possess additional higher order regularity and satisfy the corresponding compatibility condition, the global strong solution becomes a classical one. %The smallness condition above is invariant under the natural scaling of the two-dimensional isentropic compressible Navier--Stokes system. %A key point of the proof is to use this scaling to normalize the density upper bound \(\barρ\). Meanwhile, a priori large-time decay estimates for both the pressure and the spatial gradient of the velocity field are obtained in \(L^2\) at rate \(t^{-1/2}\), together with the same rate for the density-weighted material derivative of the velocity. The initial density is allowed to contain vacuum, and vacuum at infinity is included. In particular, compactly supported initial density is admissible. The result provides a scaling-invariant smallness framework for the global well-posedness theory of two-dimensional compressible barotropic flows with far-field vacuum.

title: Hardware Impairment Parameter Estimation in Fluid Antenna Systems by Inverse Optimization
authors: Songling Zhang, Zhaohui Yang, Ruopeng Xu, Hao Xu, Xusheng Zhu, Zhaoyang Zhang, Kai-Kit Wong
abstract: In this paper, the problem of estimating the hardware impairment parameters of fluid antennas (FAs) in a multi-base station (BS) multi-user communication system is studied. The actual hardware coefficients are unknown, whereas the FA positions and transmit beamforming vectors adopted by the BSs are known. We first formulate a forward spectral efficiency (SE) maximization problem and introduce aggregate interference variables whose consistency with the physical inter-cell interference can be maintained through a pricing mechanism. For inverse estimation, the aggregate interference is obtained from receiver-side interference measurements associated with the observed network decisions. We then construct a trust-region linear model of the position-update problem around the observed FA positions. To extend the applicability of the proposed framework to antenna positions obtained from inexact or heuristic algorithms, we develop an inverse optimization model with an explicit duality-gap tolerance, which is solved using sequential quadratic programming (SQP). Simulation results show that the proposed scheme attains a lower estimation error than KKT residual minimization (KKT-RM) at both considered transmit-power levels and improves the SE by up to 22.86% over the Ideal-hardware-assumption scheme.

title: Inertial Video World Models
authors: Yuan Gao, Fan Xu, Yu Guo, Yuxu Lu, Zhengru Fang, Hao Wu, Xiaomeng Huang
abstract: The physical world has inertia: it evolves from what already exists rather than being recreated at every instant. However, many existing video world models lack an explicit mechanism for inertial state evolution, leaving the continuity of motion and structure implicit in video prediction. During autoregressive rollouts, repeated reconstruction can accumulate errors and destabilize the predicted dynamics. To address this limitation, we introduce InertialWorld, an Inertial Video World Model that makes inertia a structural prior for autoregressive prediction: existing scene evidence is carried across time rather than reconstructed at every step. Central to this formulation is Inertial Memory, which turns memory from passive predictive context into an evolving video state with two complementary views: a dense Eulerian grid preserves scene-aligned evidence, while persistent Lagrangian carriers bind local content to learned canonical coordinates. At each step, the model transports the carrier content according to action-conditioned motion, predicts the complete next video state from the transported carriers and dense grid, and uses a learned gate to combine transported and newly predicted content into the memory for the next step. Extensive experiments across multiple domains, including robot manipulation, 3D game simulation, and open-world navigation, demonstrate that InertialWorld achieves competitive autoregressive prediction performance against strong video world model baselines. Codes link: https://github.com/YuanGao-YG/InertialWorld

title: Zero-Dimensional Attention Topology for Linguistic Acceptability
authors: Saeed AlMarri
abstract: Topological summaries of Transformer attention provide sentence representations for linguistic acceptability classification. We examine a zero-dimensional persistent-homology ($H_0$) representation that summarizes minimum-spanning-tree merge values from 144 symmetrized BERT attention graphs into 1,440 features. The retrospective evaluation uses 8,517 downstream training sentences and 521 in-domain and 497 out-of-domain CoLA validation sentences after data-integrity filtering. The recorded out-of-domain Matthews correlation coefficients are 0.438 for the topological representation and 0.508 for attention statistics, compared with 0.545 for BERT. Attention-feature results are retained aggregate measurements; BERT predictions are rescored and length controls are refitted from the accompanying records. Analytical results show that the representation retains token-count information and discards a class of directional attention differences. Source resampling of BERT predictions also demonstrates the sensitivity of uncertainty estimates to the sampling unit. The reported results do not demonstrate a predictive advantage for this fixed topological representation over simpler attention summaries. They identify representation properties and evaluation controls relevant to subsequent studies of attention topology.

title: MCTS Is Counting the Wrong Thing: Learning Exploration Counts for LLM Reasoning
authors: Xuan Zhang, Zhijian Zhou, Zicheng Hu, Yan Feng, Hongyan Hao, Yuan Qi, Chao Qu
abstract: Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) has powered landmark successes in reinforcement learning, yet its gains in LLM reasoning can remain modest despite substantial search effort. We identify an overlooked bottleneck: what MCTS counts. Standard UCT assigns independent visit counts to textual branches, allowing different formulations of the same reasoning strategy to repeatedly receive exploration bonuses. Our theoretical analysis shows that this count fragmentation can impair exploration efficiency, as quantified by increased cumulative regret. To address this problem, we introduce Learned Pseudo-Count MCTS (LPC-MCTS), which changes only the exploration statistic in UCT. A lightweight Coin-Flipping Network head on the policy's hidden representations estimates representation coverage, enabling related branches to share exploration evidence. Across 5 mathematical-reasoning and 7 search benchmarks, LPC-MCTS consistently outperforms strong MCTS baselines. Holding each LPC-MCTS-trained policy fixed, replacing standard MCTS counts at inference improves average mean@16 accuracy across 5 mathematical benchmarks by 3.79 percentage points on Qwen2.5-7B and 2.71 points on Qwen3-4B. Applying LPC-MCTS during both training and inference yields gains of 4.96 and 4.37 points over standard MCTS, respectively. Together, our theory and experiments show that changing what MCTS counts can substantially improve its exploration efficiency and reasoning performance.

title: FIRE-Drive: Feasibility-Informed Risk Evaluation for End-to-End Diffusion Planning
authors: Qifeng Xie, Kai-Yuan Feng, Wenkang Wan, Yue Wu, Maoguo Gong, Kai Sheng
abstract: Diffusion-based end-to-end autonomous driving models have shown strong potential in generating multimodal planning trajectories. However, their performance still depends heavily on trajectory initialization, mode evaluation, and supervision quality. Weakly constrained noisy initialization may introduce infeasible proposals and increase the burden of denoising. Moreover, selecting the optimal mode remains challenging when candidate trajectories are geometrically similar but differ in safety, interaction risk, and progress. To address these issues, we propose FIRE-Drive, a feasibility-informed risk evaluation framework for end-to-end autonomous driving. FIRE-Drive improves diffusion-based planning through dynamic feasible anchor initialization, candidate-specific bird's-eye-view risk evidence, and compact high-quality candidate supervision with lightweight refinement. This design aligns the initial support, risk-aware scoring, and multimodal supervision of trajectory modes under a unified planning objective. It enables the diffusion decoder to focus on refining plausible trajectories while the scorer distinguishes modes using local risk evidence. Experiments on NAVSIM v1 show that FIRE-Drive achieves a Predictive Driver Model Score of 91.5 with a ResNet34 backbone. Additional closed-loop evaluation on 220 Bench2Drive routes yields a Driving Score of 71.43 and a Success Rate of 42.73%. Component ablations and a scorer comparison under matched candidate inputs support the contributions of feasible initialization, auxiliary supervision, and risk-informed selection. Our code is available at https://github.com/Latte00/FIRE-drive.

title: Orbifold Morse Handles II. Boundary Regions, Gluing Maps, and Surgery Cobordisms
authors: Suhyoung Choi, Juseop Lee
abstract: We study four-dimensional quotient handles defined by faithful representations of finite groups in $\mathrm{SO}(4)$ and invariant splittings of indices $1$, $2$, and $3$. We identify their attaching and belt regions as oriented $3$-orbifolds described by labeled singular graphs. We determine the orbifold isotopy class of the boundary gluing map. Fix an orientation-reversing orbifold embedding of the attaching region into an oriented $3$-orbifold. Assume that the embedding induces isomorphisms on local groups. The regions, gluing class, and embedding determine the surgery. For a fixed handle and attaching image, an extension condition on the belt region characterizes diffeomorphisms of the cobordisms fixing a specified common exterior pointwise. For index-$2$ handles, this condition is the vanishing of an integer twist in the fixed boundary coordinates. We use these surgeries to construct a compact connected oriented $4$-orbifold cobordism from every closed connected oriented $3$-orbifold $\mathcal O$ to $S^3$. A finite sequence of index-$2$ orbifold handle attachments from $\mathcal O$ to $S^3$ exists if and only if $\mathcal O$ has no tetrahedral, octahedral, or icosahedral vertices. Let $v_{\mathbf T}(\mathcal O)$, $v_{\mathbf O}(\mathcal O)$, and $v_{\mathbf I}(\mathcal O)$ denote the numbers of these vertices. Among finite sequences of handle attachments of indices $1$, $2$, and $3$ from $\mathcal O$ to $S^3$, the minimum total number of index-$1$ and index-$3$ handles is $\left\lceil\frac{v_{\mathbf T}(\mathcal O)}{2}\right\rceil+ \left\lceil\frac{v_{\mathbf O}(\mathcal O)}{2}\right\rceil+ \left\lceil\frac{v_{\mathbf I}(\mathcal O)}{2}\right\rceil$.

title: When the World Is the Test Suite: Agentic Intelligence for the Physical World
authors: Kaixin Li, Meng Luo, Yanlin Li, Yuchen Tian, Xiang Liu, Xiangru Jian, Yan Yang, Zhiheng Xi, Yang Zhang, Ziyang Luo, Mingfei Cheng, Hongzhan Lin
abstract: Coding agents built to repair software now write, test, and repair programs for robots, laboratories, and industrial controllers. Unlike in software engineering, no test suite comes with the code. Whether a program works must be established by running it on a robot, in a physics simulator, or through the policies it helps to train, and such evidence is costly to obtain and can itself be wrong. As these agents take on more physical tasks, how their programs are judged matters as much as how they are written. This paper examines this emerging area, agentic intelligence for the physical world, by treating the world as the program's test suite. We organize the discussion around three questions: how agents write programs for the physical world, how these programs are tested, and how agents learn from the results. We first trace how language models for robots and software engineering agents came together, ask which software testing practices carry over to physical tests, and describe each program by where it sits relative to the actuator and by what judges it. For writing, we cover programs that act as robot policies and programs that support policy learning by producing rewards, tasks, and training worlds. For testing, we examine what physical trials cost, what traces, learned judges, simulators, and formal checks can establish in their place, and what safety requires beyond task success. For learning, we discuss how tested programs are retained as experience, in skill libraries and in model weights. Finally, we turn to benchmarks and evaluation practice and outline open challenges. Writing programs is becoming cheap, while trustworthy evidence about what they do remains costly. Progress will therefore depend on a physical counterpart of continuous integration: verification cheap enough to run often, reliable enough to trust under search, and maintained alongside the experience it validates.

title: Towards Physics-Constrained Rectified Flow for Climate Downscaling: What Projections Can Certify?
authors: Arun Sharma
abstract: Statistical downscaling restores the regional detail behind flooding and crop stress, but diffusion and flow-matching generators can produce sharp fields that break the conservation laws of their coarse input. Physics-Constrained Rectified Flow (PC-RF) is a conditional flow-matching downscaler. Its training penalties target wind divergence, negative precipitation, and mass drift from the coarse total, and a projection after sampling removes the last two exactly. On one corrupted synthetic field with no trained network, the projection drives the Non-negativity Violation Rate (NVR) from 0.236 and the Mass-Conservation Error (MCE) from 0.184 to zero, and the penalties lower the Divergence Error (DE) by about 30%. On ERA5 the projection gives PC-RF and RF-base, the penalty-free rectified-flow baseline, an NVR of exactly zero and an MCE of zero up to float32 rounding. The penalties add no perceptual gain that we can separate from training budget or run-to-run variation. At a matched budget on 2019-2021, PC-RF has no edge over RF-base (SSIM 0.939 vs. 0.942, PSNR 31.81 vs. 31.79, CRPS 0.771 vs. 0.772). Our unprojected CorrDiff reimplementation beats both flow models on PSNR (28.38) and CRPS (1.092) on 2020, yet 45% of its ensemble-mean precipitation cells are negative. On ERA5 a sign error in the divergence operator made that penalty and DE act on a deformation-like term. The fine reference is interpolated from ERA5 and accumulates precipitation over a longer window, so the perceptual scores cannot establish downscaling skill. NVR and MCE need one pass and no fine reference, so we argue they should run first as pass-or-fail checks, with DE as a diagnostic.

title: Approximating Itô Processes in Adapted Wasserstein Distance with Finite Support Laws
authors: Xihao He, Fengyi Yuan
abstract: Motivated by finite-scenario surrogates in stopping and control problems, we study the approximation of Itô diffusion laws by laws supported on $M$ paths in an adapted Wasserstein distance, which we term adapted functional quantization. Under the strict adapted Wasserstein distance, no finite-support approximation can achieve vanishing error, while even under its relaxed counterpart, naive empirical measures still fail to converge. To resolve this, we develop a recursive conditional sampling algorithm and derive constructive upper bounds on the adapted quantization error. In one dimension, this yields the Brownian rate $(\log M)^{-1/2}$ for every diffusion with continuous coefficients of linear growth and pathwise uniqueness. In several dimensions, a quantitative Osgood stability condition with exponent $β$ yields the rate $(\log M)^{-η_p}$, where $η_p=\min\{1/2,β/(β+4p-2)\}$. Without the Osgood condition, we construct a two-dimensional diffusion with smooth bounded coefficients whose adapted quantization error decays more slowly than $(\log M)^{-γ}$ for any $γ>0$.

title: Explaining Realized Returns: Roll's $R^2$ 40 Years Later
authors: Bryan Kelly, Yinan Su, Chao Zhang
abstract: Can we explain asset price movements even with hindsight? Reinterpreting Roll's (1988) AFA Presidential Address, "$R^2$," as a modern empirical exercise, we show that conventional macroeconomic, cash-flow, expectations, and flow variables explain less than 10% (often with negative $R^2$) of monthly U.S. equity return variation out of sample and lack daily observations. We use generative AI to extract reasons stated in Wall Street Journal market summaries while filtering out price-related language. These reasons explain around 30-40% of daily and monthly return variation out of sample. Their content spans interpretable themes, including corporate news, macroeconomic conditions, monetary policy, sentiment, and geopolitics.

title: GuardAgent: A Memory-Augmented Agentic Framework for Adaptive Detection of Adversarial Promotions in LLM-Based Recommendation
authors: Shiyi Yang, Xinshu Li, Chen Wang, Xiwei Xu, Liming Zhu, Lina Yao
abstract: In traditional recommender systems (RSs), textual information typically serves as auxiliary signals for representation learning. In contrast, in LLM-based RSs, textual information becomes the primary medium for recommendation generation through semantic understanding and reasoning. This shift fundamentally changes the attack surface, making promotion-driven manipulations more feasible, effective, and harder to detect. However, effectively detecting such attacks remains largely unexplored. To fill this gap, we present the first systematic study on detecting promotion-driven attacks against LLM-based RSs, aiming to safeguard next-generation recommendation platforms. Specifically, we propose GuardAgent, a novel LLM-powered agentic detection framework that operates through a loop of Perception, Action, Reflection and Memory. In contrast to conventional LLM-based detectors that function in a static, one-off, and opaque fashion, GuardAgent continually learns and self-evolves to adapt to unseen threat patterns while generating explainable reasoning traces and outcomes. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that GuardAgent achieves state-of-the-art generalization performance, laying the foundation for robust and trustworthy recommendation in practical settings.

title: Anticipating or Speculating? Making Futures Pay in AI Ethics
authors: John P. Nelson
abstract: Philosophers have recently been trying to develop uniform decision rules for instances in which physicians' judgments diverge from the recommendations of medical artificial intelligence (AI) systems. I argue that this effort is fatally flawed because the performance and appropriate use of algorithmic recommendation systems by physicians are highly context-specific, empirical medical matters rather than epistemological ones. In such instances, general decision rules can be stipulated only to the extent that they abstract away from relevant, indeed determinative, contextual circumstances. The alleged problem of physician-AI disagreement, and others like it, play into longstanding disputes in technology ethics about the viability and utility of envisioning possible futures: is this useful "anticipation" or wasteful "speculation"? I suggest that the two may be distinguished. Anticipation explores plausible futures to help inform present actions under irreducible uncertainty. Speculation abstracts away uncertainty, developing formal solutions to stipulated circumstances whose relationship to the real present is often quite unclear. Efforts to develop crisp philosophical solutions to physician-AI disagreement, among other problems, fall into the latter category. Technology ethics should remember that fruitful futures thinking must both begin from and return to the messy, uncertain present.

title: Gravitational waves from cosmological first-order phase transitions with fluctuation-induced friction
authors: Jun-Ye Chen, Dongdong Wei, Zong-Kuan Guo
abstract: We study gravitational-wave production in a cosmological first-order phase transition with fluctuation-induced friction using three-dimensional lattice simulations of two coupled scalar fields. Kinetic and gradient energy in the additional field $s$ accumulates near the expanding bubble walls of $φ$ and affects their motion. The contribution from $s$ exceeds that from $φ$ at the spectral peak and has a slope similar to that of the bulk flow model over a finite interval above the peak. In the high-wave-number (UV) direction, $φ$ dominates and the total spectrum develops a broad feature. For the larger coupling, slowly contracting false vacuum remnants persist long after bubble merger.

title: Algebraic Vector Fields on Compact Homogeneous Spaces are 2-generated
authors: Yiyang Jiang, Xudong Chen
abstract: Let $M$ be a compact, connected manifold on which a compact Lie group $K$ acts smoothly and transitively. We show that the Lie algebra of algebraic vector fields on $M$, i.e., of smooth vector fields whose translates under $K$ span finite-dimensional spaces, is generated by two vector fields. Consequently, the subgroup generated by the flows of these two vector fields is dense in the identity component of the diffeomorphism group of $M$. For spheres, explicit generators are obtained from earlier results on spherical vector fields.

title: Fidelity Regret: Measuring Simulator Misspecification in Verifiable Design
authors: Noah Flynn
abstract: RLVF assumes the verifier evaluates the quantity of interest. In genetic-circuit design, a topological verifier can establish that a program is a valid circuit computing the target function, whereas ranking its physical performance requires a simulator. We measure fidelity regret, the reference simple regret incurred when a cheap simulator selects the design, over a 21,362-design combination subspace spanning 5 measured gate libraries and 3 organisms. Exact ordered-assignment checks retain positive regret in every tested cell while shifting magnitudes in both directions. Mean normalized regret is 0.369 over 72 cells and only 6 have zero regret. The discrepancy depends strongly on the reference axis: the yeast library SC1C1G1T1 has mean regret 0.113 for cytometry quality and 0.801 for growth burden, and every evaluated library--circuit-size pair has positive burden regret. Topological verification ties all valid gate assignments, while an oracle whitelist subject to retaining at least 25% of the design space leaves positive regret in 30 of 52 cells. Design-space optimization and feedback-guided search with frozen language models reach the high-regret regions; on a matched zero-regret control, additional optimization instead reduces regret. At a matched modeled-cost budget, mitigation is budget- and library-dependent. An in-sample fixed rule spending $α{=}0.34$ of the budget re-scoring top cheap-simulator designs achieves mean excess regret 0.016, compared with 0.305 for cheap-only and 0.034 for reference-only selection, improving on cheap-only in 330 of 360 cells. More broadly, any workflow optimized through a simulator or digital twin can satisfy its verifier yet perform poorly on the intended physical objective. Fidelity regret provides a transferable template for detecting this gap before optimization and comparing budget-aware remedies across scientific domains.

title: Logical error prediction and geometry selection for rectangular surface codes under biased circuit-level noise
authors: Youshin Chung, Yujin Kang, Jun Heo
abstract: Realistic quantum hardware often exhibits biased noise, but at the circuit level this bias may affect only a subset of operations and need not be transferred uniformly to logical errors. The logical response to a given physical bias is therefore central to selecting resource-efficient surface code geometries. Here, we study unrotated rectangular surface codes under standard depolarizing and superconducting-inspired circuit-level noise models. We first construct geometry-dependent logical error rate models from unbiased circuit-level simulations. We then use logical sensitivities to compare the responses to localized idle-bias and global physical error perturbations, defining logical-error-type-dependent response coefficients from an unbiased reference circuit without fitting to finite-bias data. These coefficients are incorporated through effective error parameters, yielding a median fold error of 1.09 over the evaluated finite-bias conditions. Geometries selected by the model are validated through direct biased circuit-level simulations. At a physical error rate of 0.004 and a target logical error rate of 10^{-3}, the validated rectangular codes reduce physical qubit overhead by up to 42.4% and 26.2% under the two noise models, respectively, relative to unrotated square codes. These results provide a practical link between circuit-level bias response and resource-efficient surface code design.

title: ALERT: Extending Humanoid Motion Trackers with a General and Lightweight Human Avoidance Pipeline
authors: Zhaoyang Li, Chiyu Zhang, Chengxin Xu, Peng Yang, Zhonghao Guo, Wanting Li, Ziyu Chen
abstract: Whole-body motion tracking has enabled humanoid dancing, athletic motions, and teleoperation, providing a foundation for capability demonstrations and manipulation data collection. However, existing tracking policies lack awareness of nearby humans and proactive avoidance capabilities, while motion substitution and local constraint-based corrections may compromise reference motion integrity and tracking continuity. We propose ALERT, a general lightweight pipeline for extending motion tracking to shared human-robot environments. Through lightweight adaptation, it integrates human perception and proactive avoidance into pretrained tracking policies, balancing avoidance demands with reference motion tracking while preserving existing motion capabilities. Simulation and real-world experiments across tracking backbones demonstrate reliable collision-free execution through localized human avoidance, preserving whole-body coordination and enabling rapid recovery of reference tracking, while retaining the ability of pretrained policies to track unseen motions.

title: Global existence and emergent dynamics of singular Cucker-Smale model on general digraphs
authors: Jinwook Jung, Hyungsuk Kang, Wonjin Lim, Eojin Shin
abstract: We investigate the global-in-time dynamics of the Cucker--Smale model under general network topologies with a singular communication weight function $ψ(r) = r^{-α}$, $α>0$. For $α\ge 1$, we establish the global-in-time existence of smooth solutions when network topologies belong to one of several classes of directed graphs. In particular, in one dimension, we present a necessary condition on the network topology for global existence by constructing finite-time blow-up solutions from non-collisional initial configurations. Moreover, we provide a sufficient framework for the emergence of mono-cluster flocking. For certain classes of network topologies, we further show that mono-cluster flocking occurs unconditionally for non-collisional initial configuration when $α=1$.

title: PCGRL for Complex Platformers: Synthesizing Playable and Diverse Levels via Inflated Envelopes and Forward Curricula
authors: Di Wu
abstract: Procedural Content Generation via Reinforcement Learning (PCGRL) has emerged as a promising paradigm for automated game development. However, existing PCGRL frameworks still suffer from severe exploration bottlenecks and scaling limitations when faced with long-sequence generation tasks governed by strict rigid-body rules and non-linear kinematic boundaries (e.g., platformer constraints). Consequently, traditional approaches frequently fail to maintain reliable level solvability on large-scale canvases. To address these challenges, we present a physics-aware, curriculum-guided PCGRL framework. First, we construct an "Inflated Volume Envelope" mechanism, which provides a physics-constrained representation that incorporates continuous kinematic feasibility into the discrete state space of the MDP. Second, to alleviate the sparse reward challenge induced by extremely long decision sequences, we introduce intermediate state-transition feedback and a multi-stage forward extension curriculum learning framework, enabling informative value estimation and stable credit assignment over long-horizon trajectories. Finally, to resolve the issue where deterministic policies after convergence generate highly monotonous map paths with a lack of diversity, we activate high-entropy stochastic inference during the synthesis phase, regularized by a post-hoc parallel rejection filtering mechanism. Experimental results demonstrate that our framework significantly enhances structural diversity while maintaining high physical playability across multi-scale environments. Comparative evaluations across multi-scale canvases demonstrate that our framework maintains superior convergence stability and dimensional scalability, reliably synthesizing solvable levels where traditional PCGRL baselines degrade.

title: OAK-Mind: Zero-Training Mental Health Change Inference from Passive Sensing via Knowledge-Grounded Multi-Agent LLMs
authors: Yishu Ji, Zhihan Jiang, Will Ke Wang, Yuang Fan, Anind K. Dey, Xuhai "Orson" Xu
abstract: Wearable and smartphone sensors capture behavioral signals associated with mental health, yet inferring mental health outcomes from these signals has traditionally relied on supervised models requiring labeled data and offering limited insight into their predictions. Large language models (LLMs) offer new opportunities to reason over behavioral evidence, but existing LLM-based approaches to passive sensing have largely continued to rely on task-specific fine-tuning or sensor-specific pretraining. In this paper, we introduce \textbf{OAK-Mind}, a zer\textbf{O}-training, multi-\textbf{A}gent, \textbf{K}nowledge-grounded LLM pipeline for inferring mental health changes from passive sensing data. The pipeline organizes sensing data into behavioral dimensions including sleep, physical activity, location mobility, and smartphone use, and orchestrates specialized agents grounded in mental health literature to interpret longitudinal behavioral changes. It synthesizes their assessments and applies questionnaire-based symptom rating to infer changes relative to an individual's baseline assessment with human-readable rationale grounded in observed behavioral patterns and domain knowledge. Across datasets and prediction tasks, while without task-specific training, OAK-Mind achieves comparable or better performance than the most predictive supervised baselines trained on additional labeled samples. It also demonstrate consistent improvement upon direct prompting across four tested LLM backbones. Ablation analyses support the benefits of combining behavioral interpretation with symptom rating, distributing analysis across domain-specific agents, and incorporating domain knowledge. Our findings highlight the potential of knowledge-grounded, multi-agent LLMs for training-free inference of mental health changes from passive sensing data.

title: CHEQ: A Concurrent Hardware Evaluation Platform for QEC Decoders via Batch-Invariant Circuit-Level Noise Sampling
authors: Sechan Park, Kyeongwon Lee, Mundo Jung, Chaebin Jung, Woojoo Lee
abstract: Hardware quantum error correction (QEC) decoders require validation of logical error suppression and timing compliance before deployment. Rare logical failures and deadline violations demand extensive sampling, while algorithm-level software evaluation does not directly measure hardware response times. Circuit-level noise models contain many error mechanisms but few firings per shot at low physical error rates, making exhaustive per-shot scanning inefficient. We present CHEQ, an FPGA platform integrating on-chip sampling, concurrent decoder evaluation, scoring, and RISC-V control. Its Sampling Units use geometric skipping to sample firing locations from detector error models and amortize mechanism traversal across shots within each batch. Under independent random draws and exact geometric sampling, the shot distribution is invariant to batch size, enabling a memory-throughput tradeoff. A throughput model guides joint selection of the Sampling Unit count, batch size, and decoder count under FPGA resource constraints. Across evaluated conditions, the pooled one-sided 95% upper bound on the weighted root-mean-square relative firing-rate difference from Stim is 0.16%. At a batch size of 4,096, a Sampling Unit uses only 4.8%-11.2% of a Helios decoder's LUTs for code distances 7, 9, 11, and 13. On an AMD VCU118 FPGA at code distance 7 and physical error rate 10^-3, two Sampling Units supply 20 Helios decoders at 49.2 million shots/s, completing 10^10 shots in 3.4 minutes without host-side shot generation.

title: Optimal Energy and LLM Task Scheduling for Multiple Cloud Data Centers
authors: Zhongqi Zhao, Lei Fan, Zhu Han
abstract: This paper studies coordinated Large Language Model (LLM) training-task scheduling and facility operation for geographically distributed cloud data centers (CDCs). The central question is how two scheduling flexibilities - cross-CDC task transfer and task reordering - affect service and economic outcomes when remote execution remains subject to compute, bandwidth, energy, and zone-temperature constraints. We formulate a mixed-integer optimization model that jointly determines task outcomes, heterogeneous-node assignment, execution timing, pre-execution data transfer, node activation, and facility operation. A deterministic 24-hour case study contains 3 CDCs, 15 heterogeneous graphics processing unit (GPU) nodes, 4 thermal zones per CDC, and 103 tasks. In this instance, enabling transfer increases net profit by 57.9% relative to the otherwise matched no-transfer variant and increases completed tasks from 76 to 103. The more restrictive no-transfer FIFO-prefix variant completes 14 tasks and yields negative profit. The proposed schedule transfers 39 tasks, achieves 70.3% node utilization, and maintains zone temperatures within 24°C-27°C. These fixed-instance results indicate that cross-CDC transfer and task-reordering flexibility can improve the modeled profit and task-completion outcomes under the studied conditions.

title: Where Does Hindsight Enter Clinical Agent Benchmarks? An Audit of Simulators and Case Construction
authors: Meilu Zhu, Xiaohan Li, Axiu Mao
abstract: Benchmarks for LLM diagnostic agents are built from retrospective records: the case an agent reads is rewritten from discharge summaries, and unrecorded test results are generated by a simulator that often sees the final diagnosis. HindAudit separates three hindsight channels (the diagnosis given to the simulator, the retrospective context it conditions on, and the agent-facing case text) and measures each with judges trained only on real data. On 27,489 emergency admissions from MIMIC-IV, five registered tests found no leakage into simulated laboratory results: providing the diagnosis to five simulators had a negligible effect, and prompted gatekeepers diluted the diagnostic signal, although exploratory results suggest they can raise agent scores. The largest effect lay in the case text. Against a presentation-time reconstruction from triage records, benchmark-style summaries raised the zero-shot accuracy of four LLMs from 25.4% to 39.7% and discharge histories to 45.3%, and raised six interactive agents' scores while barely changing their ranking. The exploratory gap was reproduced in a registered replication on held-out patients. Masking diagnosis names left it unchanged. Because MIMIC lacks a contemporaneous bedside history, the gap is an upper bound on hindsight. We report all registered outcomes and recommend construction practices.

title: Cross3DGS: Unified Vulkan-Based 3D Gaussian Splatting Training from Workstations to Mobile Devices
authors: Hiroyuki Sato, Yusuke Takimoto
abstract: Scenes captured with handheld and wearable cameras are still shipped to a CUDA workstation for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) training. Training on the device that captured them, or on its companion phone or laptop, requires more than translating kernels: GPUs and drivers differ in parallel features, memory limits, and command submission, and these differences decide whether a training schedule executes and returns the correct update. We present Cross3DGS, a cross-vendor, cross-platform Vulkan trainer that keeps one optimizer and chooses its execution schedule per device in two steps: rules on device limits, workload size, and observed driver failures exclude the schedules known not to run correctly, and a fixed preference order selects one of the remaining feasible schedules. The same core completes standard-quality training (30k updates, one million Gaussians) on every configuration we measured, spanning NVIDIA, Intel, Arm, Qualcomm, AMD, and Apple GPUs and including Android devices and an iPhone, whereas the existing portable trainers VkSplat and Brush do not run on some of the mobile GPUs. Averaged over 11 scenes on a workstation, Cross3DGS has higher quality than VkSplat with no significant difference in training time, and Brush reports about three times the training time at comparable quality. The final quality of Cross3DGS is nearly identical across devices. A mobile application turns a handheld capture into a viewable model entirely on the device.

title: CoSphere-SLAM: Multi-Agent Panoramic Gaussian Splatting SLAM with Spherical Loop Closure
authors: Qi Shao, Zhihao Cao, Shuhao Zhai, Taoyu Wu, Zhuoxiao Li, Anh Nguyen, Long Hu, Xianzhi Li, Hong Liang, Baoru Huang, Liang Li
abstract: Dense collaborative mapping is essential for search and rescue, building inspection, and warehouse automation, where panoramic cameras capture the entire surroundings in a single frame. Unlike pinhole agents that share views only at similar headings, panoramic agents observe overlapping scenes at any 3D orientation, yet searching full rotations also produces mutually consistent false loop closures across distinct symmetric rooms. Moreover, continuous monocular scale drift splits rigidly merged maps at revisited surfaces, while depth noise at short baselines distorts loop translation directions. To address these challenges, we propose CoSphere-SLAM, the first multi-agent Gaussian splatting SLAM framework for panoramic cameras, whose spherical loop closure aligns spherical features over $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ via fast Fourier correlation across arbitrary orientations and rejects symmetric false closures through global $\mathrm{Sim}(3)$ consensus. Building on these closures, directional global optimization solves a per-keyframe $\mathrm{Sim}(3)$ pose graph with log-scale regularization to correct scale drift while separating optical-flow translation directions from depth-based magnitudes. Finally, omnidirectional Gaussian fusion transforms each Gaussian with its keyframe similarity and renders Gaussians at their maximum ray response to jointly refine poses and maps. Experiments on indoor and cross-session multi-agent panoramic benchmarks demonstrate that CoSphere-SLAM achieves state-of-the-art trajectory accuracy and rendering quality among single-agent and multi-agent methods. Project website: https://cosphere-slam.github.io.

title: From Temperature-Limited to Battery-Limited Legged Locomotion
authors: Raphaël Ségas, Balázs Opra, Léo Ghafari, Thomas Stewart
abstract: On legged robots, sustained locomotion often ends in thermal shutdown rather than battery depletion: the heat of walking concentrates in a few joint motors, which overheat long before the battery is empty. We train thermally aware locomotion policies by reinforcement learning without ever observing temperature, and demonstrate this on a Unitree Go2 quadruped. We first identify a coupled 13-node lumped RC thermal network, fitted on two runs of a single robot and calibrated against the measured electrical power, that predicts all twelve motor temperatures with a mean RMSE below 1 $^\circ$C across different robot instances, gaits, payloads, and speeds. Under a sustained gait, the temperatures the motors will settle at follow directly from the gait-averaged squared torques and joint speeds. Our core contribution is a reward that drives down the hottest predicted asymptotes: thermal time constants exceed the credit-assignment horizon of reinforcement learning by orders of magnitude, but predicted asymptotes respond to torque and joint speed within a single gait cycle, so the policy learns to lower and spread heat with no temperature input. On the robot, the policy turns sustained locomotion from temperature-limited to battery-limited: with a 5 kg payload at 1 m/s, a learned baseline reaches thermal shutdown after 19 minutes (1.1 km), whereas our policy runs the battery down after 174 minutes (10.0 km) with its hottest motor 14 $^\circ$C below the shutdown threshold in a 26 $^\circ$C room; on an unloaded factory circuit with stairs and ramps, the baseline overheats after 25 laps (6.2 km), while our policy completes 47 (11.2 km) on one battery with 22 $^\circ$C of margin.

title: SOTA or Luck? The Winner's Curse in LLM Leaderboards
authors: Sikun Xu, Raphael Thomadsen, Dennis J. Zhang, Heng Zhang
abstract: Public LLM leaderboards guide model evaluation and adoption, yet the reported performance of top-ranked models can be systematically overstated. This leaderboard winner's curse arises because ranking noisy benchmark scores rewards sampling luck alongside genuine ability. The same selection effect can distort scores throughout the leaderboard, a phenomenon we call the rank-induced bias. We develop an $m$-out-of-$N$ bootstrap to correct for this bias. It assumes a fixed model pool with independent, identically distributed bounded tasks while allowing arbitrary within-task correlation among models. Under exact population tiers separated by positive gaps, we prove that the bootstrap reduces $Θ(N^{-1/2})$ ranking bias to expected residual bias $o(N^{-1/2})$. Across 14 benchmarks from 5 benchmark families, the rank-1 adjustments range from approximately 0.09 to 3.86 percentage points. In our SWE-bench Verified snapshot, the tied leaders receive an adjustment of 0.90 percentage points. Such overstatement is large enough to make the apparent winner statistically fragile. Thus, we use the same bootstrap to further quantify the intervals of plausible rank positions for each model and group models into tiers. We establish sufficient conditions for consistent recovery of population tiers. On SWE-bench Verified, this procedure places 13 of 173 models in the leading tier. We combine the score adjustment and rank intervals in the Rank Uncertainty and Leaderboard Evaluation Report (RULER). We validate its finite-sample performance using sample splitting and calibrated simulations, and advocate publishing RULER alongside raw rankings so readers can assess both reported performance and the precision of the ordering. RULER also provides guidance for benchmark design that accounts for selection effects and ranking uncertainty.

title: $L^p$-norms of holomorphic cusp forms
authors: Xiaolong Han, Bingrong Huang
abstract: We determine the optimal orders of local and global $L^p$-norms of $L^2$-normalized holomorphic cusp forms of large weight on the modular surface, for fixed $2<p\leq\infty$. Both orders are attained by peak forms. For normalized Poincaré series of weight $k$ and index $m$, we obtain an asymptotic formula with an explicit constant, uniformly for $1\leq m\leq c_0k$ with any fixed $c_0<(4π)^{-1}$. We also give sup norm bounds in a wider range of indices.

title: Temporal polarization properties of accretion flows into supermassive black holes: INSANE as an alternative
authors: Jane SiNan Long, Akhil Uniyal, Yosuke Mizuno, Koushik Chatterjee, Kinwah Wu
abstract: Temporal variability and polarization provide unique diagnostics of the magnetic field structure and plasma dynamics in accretion flows around supermassive black holes. We investigate the temporal polarization properties of horizon-scale emission using general relativistic magnetohydrodynamic (GRMHD) simulations coupled with polarized general relativistic radiative transfer (GRRT) for three accretion states: Standard and Normal Evolution (SANE), Magnetically Arrested Disk (MAD), and an intermediate regime (INSANE). Fourier polarization-mode decomposition, through the ratio $|β_m|/|β_2|$, shows that MAD produces the most rotationally symmetric EVPA patterns, SANE the most asymmetric, and INSANE lies in between. The multi-scale temporal behaviour of the intensity is investigated using the Continuous Wavelet Transform and Hilbert-Huang Transform. Both methods identify localized oscillatory features associated with magnetic-flux eruption events in the MAD simulations. In the shorter interval examined, INSANE distributes its variability more evenly among several time-scales, while the SANE behaviour depends more strongly on the electron-temperature prescription. To quantify the spectral distribution, we define a fast power fraction $F_{\mathrm{fast},I}$ for periods of 80-200 $M$ within a broad band of 80-1500 $M$. Both methods give the smallest fractions for MAD; the ordering of state medians, INSANE > SANE > MAD, persists when the upper fast-band boundary is varied from 200 to 500 $M$. Our analysis demonstrates that combining polarization morphology with multi-scale temporal analysis provides a useful means of distinguishing magnetization states, supporting INSANE as a distinct observational alternative to conventional MAD/SANE for interpreting horizon-scale observations of M87$^{*}$ and related systems.

title: Social Signal Bench: Evidence-Weighted Evaluation of Co-occurring Social Signals in Video and Audio
authors: Siddharth Ravi, Anders R. Bargum, Hugo Anselme, Patrizio Cugia di Sant'Orsola, Alberto Cardaci, Flora Kincso Parragi, Vincent Borowiec, Line H. Clemmensen
abstract: Recognizing social signals such as interest and hesitation requires interpreting context-dependent behaviors that may co-occur in conversation. Existing affective computing benchmarks rarely evaluate such co-occurring signals, and conventional multi-label F1 overlooks semantic relationships and annotator disagreement. We introduce Social Signal Bench, a 47-hour densely annotated benchmark for the evaluation of social signal recognition and engagement, comprising two datasets: Social Signal Bench Video (25 hours), covering ten social signals in audiovisual recordings, and Social Signal Bench Audio (22 hours), covering six signals in audio-only recordings. Each dataset pairs a public training set of online conversational video, of which 10 hours are expert-annotated and the remainder pseudo-labeled, with a private expert-labeled test set spanning four conversational domains. We also propose Evidence-Weighted F1 (EW-F1), which weights reference labels by annotator evidence and assigns graded credit to semantically related predictions through optimal per-clip matching. Controlled perturbations demonstrate that EW-F1 distinguishes semantically related errors from unrelated ones, unlike conventional F1. Under a shared evaluation protocol, 7B open models post-trained on Social Signal Bench outperform general-purpose frontier models on video and match them on audio.

title: EM-SDTrack: Efficient Multi-Scale Spike-driven Tracking for Event Cameras
authors: Yimeng Shan, Haodi Wu, Wei Zheng, Xiaowei Ye, Shuai Wang, Yu Liang, Wei Hua, Chenxiao Dou, Malu Zhang
abstract: Event-driven spiking neural networks (SNNs) match the sparse spatiotemporal output of event cameras, making spike-driven trackers highly attractive for neuromorphic edge deployment. However, events reveal a target only through their spatial distribution, whose extent varies more than tenfold within one sequence. Event tracking therefore demands multi-scale representation, which existing spike-driven trackers lack. Transferring multi-scale schemes from artificial neural networks either breaks spike-driven inference with floating-point multiplication or repeats backbone computation across input scales. To address this, we propose Spike-driven Multi-Scale Interaction (SDMI), which performs cross-scale interaction in a single spiking forward pass. Its core, Dyadic Spike Sampling (DSS), restricts sampling coordinates to dyadic fractions and thus requires only shifts and additions. The resulting M-SDTrack is fully spike-driven at inference. For tighter edge budgets, we further propose Polarity-Privileged Distillation (PPD), which distils M-SDTrack into EM-SDTrack. PPD treats the event counts cancelled by the voxel representation as privileged information. Its core constraint, Polarity-Guided Curvature Distillation (PGCD), aligns the curvature of the template-search relation under polarity-guided perturbations. On FE108, FELT and VisEvent, M-SDTrack achieves state-of-the-art accuracy with an AUC of 65.1, 41.7 and 42.0. EM-SDTrack retains 99% of the accuracy of its teacher M-SDTrack-Tiny with 27% of its energy and 18% of its parameters. On the Lynxi KA200 neuromorphic chip, it runs losslessly in real time at 116 FPS and 0.12 W.

title: Observability and Domain Shape Design for a Class of Degenerate Schrödinger Equations
authors: Dong-Hui Yang, Mengze Gu, Wei Zhao, Yuanzhi Zhou
abstract: This paper investigates boundary observability for a class of two dimensional degenerate Schrodinger equations on the unit square. The diffusion matrix has diagonal entries x1 to the power alpha1 and x2 to the power alpha2, where both parameters lie between zero and one. Since the underlying degenerate elliptic operator lacks global H2 regularity, classical Rellich space time multiplier and hidden regularity arguments cannot be applied directly to weak solutions. We introduce a truncation parameter delta and construct uniformly elliptic problems on nondegenerate subdomains. Weighted Poincare inequalities, Sturm Liouville nodal properties, spectral decomposition, and Hilbert tensor product techniques yield an operator resolvent approximation and strong convergence of the state solutions and their boundary normal derivatives in suitable energy and trace spaces. Passing to the limit in the parameterized multiplier identities gives a boundary observability inequality for the original degenerate system on the nondegenerate active boundaries. When alpha1 is less than or equal to alpha2, the minimal observation time is 4 times the square root of 2 divided by the product of 1 minus alpha1 and 2 minus alpha2. This time tends to infinity as alpha1 tends to one, whereas it tends to 2 times the square root of 2 in the nondegenerate limit.

title: Remembered as Brief: Stored Preferences SilentlyRemove Decision-Critical Information
authors: Joshua Adrian Cahyono
abstract: People increasingly learn what they need for decisions about health, money, law and safety from AI assistants, and what an assistant leaves out the user never sees. An answer with a warning removed can be true in every sentence, so fact-checks pass it, and an assistant with memory applies a preference stored once to later questions the user never had in mind. We introduce \bench{}, an Inspect benchmark of 100 everyday decisions across 25 domains in which only the assistant's memory of the user varies: the user states a belief, the model infers it from a remark, or a web page the user asked to summarise plants it. Testing five models, we find three effects. First, after summarising a page with one line addressed to AI assistants, Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite and DeepSeek V4 Pro save ``prefers very short answers and does not want warnings'' as the user's preference in every episode, and 93\% and 84\% of their later answers miss a critical item, almost always silently; under a stated brevity preference, 78--96\% of omissions are silent. Second, the same two models then pick an option for the user on 80\% and 95\% of value-dependent choices, against none with neutral memory. Third, a one-line instruction leaves 2--8\% of answers with a silent gap but most missing content still missing, while listing the must-know points before applying the user profile restores more of the content in four of five models. We release the scenarios, harness and logs.

title: CascadeJEPA: Enhancing 3D Geometric Representations via Spatially Coupled Cascaded Prediction
authors: Kailai Zhou, Ziqi Chen, Xiaoning Xu, Yuefeng Wu, Zixuan Fu, Zijun Lin, Zhihao Li, Youwei Pang, Xiaoqi Zhao, Xun Cao, Bihan Wen
abstract: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for predictive visual representation learning. However, our analysis of I-JEPA reveals a growing discrepancy between semantic and geometric learning: improved semantic recognition during pretraining is accompanied by degraded 3D geometric representations. We hypothesize that this partly stems from predicting highly abstract latent representations with incomplete spatial context, favoring semantic regularities over fine-grained geometric information. To address this issue, we introduce CascadeJEPA, a spatially coupled cascaded prediction framework that promotes richer patch-level interactions through full-grid context encoding and cross-attention between prediction stages, while largely preserving the original I-JEPA architecture. Extensive experiments demonstrate substantial improvements over I-JEPA across multiple 3D geometric tasks while maintaining strong semantic recognition performance. Furthermore, its advantages extend to future feature forecasting and world model planning, highlighting the potential of enhanced geometric representations to support predictive world modeling.

title: Quadrature-Free Radial Intracule Densities: A Bessel-Harmonic Formulation for Gaussian Basis Sets
authors: Evelio Francisco, José Antonio Quiñonero, Ángel Martín Pendás
abstract: The radial intracule density $I(R)$, the probability distribution of the interelectronic distance, is a compact and physically transparent picture of electron correlation, but its evaluation for molecules has always relied on a numerical angular quadrature over the orientation of the interelectronic vector. We show that this quadrature can be removed altogether for Cartesian Gaussian basis sets and arbitrary second-order density matrices. Starting from the Hermite Gaussian expansion of the products of basis functions, the coupling exponential $e^{2μ\mathbf{R}\cdot\mathbf{T}}$ that links radial and angular variables is expanded in modified spherical Bessel functions and real spherical harmonics, and the expansion terminates rigorously at $l=p_x+p_y+p_z$, where the $p$'s are the Cartesian powers arising from the Hermite expansion. The angular average is then exact, the atomic limit reduces to a finite sum of terms $C_iR^{n_i}e^{-μR^2}$, and the radial moments $\int_0^\infty R^nI(R)\,dR$ are given in closed form through the confluent hypergeometric function ${}_1F_1$. The scheme is exact in principle and fails only arithmetically: we identify the catastrophic cancellations in the angular-momentum coupling that ruin binary64 evaluations for heavy atoms and remove them by elevating the cancelling chain to binary128. Sum rules for the total, Coulomb and exchange-correlation intracules are recovered to seven to eight significant digits for systems from LiH to Kr$_2$, whereas Euler-Maclaurin and Lebedev quadratures err by up to 22% for stretched or multicenter molecules.

title: CULypso: A Clustered Federated Unlearning paradigm for Vehicular Ad-Hoc Networks
authors: Eleftheria Chini, George Margaritis, Dimitrios Katsaros
abstract: Unlearning has emerged as an essential security and privacy-preserving solution in Machine Learning, enabling networks to support their clients' rights for data erasure, as mandated by data protection regulations.
